en: The Poem on the Life of Siddhārtha,
a Great Poem (Mahākāvya) titled Padyacūḍāmaṇi, composed by Ācārya Buddhaghoṣa.
First Chapter:
May there be auspiciousness!
[Salutation to him] whose falling glance is rippled with compassion, and who is a dark cloud to the fire of the pride of Kandarpa.
I salute the great stalk, the kinsman of the sun, which is the root-tuber of the wish-fulfilling tree of liberation. 1.1
Even ascetics such as those seated upon lotuses were not able to speak even a single portion of it;
therefore, my desire to recount this life and heroic deeds of the Teacher is nothing but childish folly.
Nevertheless, through the power of devotion placed in him, I am skilled enough to explain this very matter;
for indeed, by taking refuge at his feet, even the dust brings prosperity to men. 1.3.
There is a certain praiseworthy city named Kapila, which grants all desires to its subjects;
beholding it, Śakra relaxes his intention to boast of his own royal capital.
In that city, the moon— the nectar-rayed one— is imagined by the women to be a lunar disc resting upon the flagstaffs of the palaces,
as if it had been impaled on a stake out of anger at the theft of the splendor of their lotus-faces.
In whose ruby-studded streets the celestial lights shine as reflections,
like pearls fallen from the bow of the bodiless God of Love as it draws them forth.
There, the lofty mansions of the wealthy, bearing aloft the poles of their victorious banners,
seem to incessantly summon supplicants with the ringing of their swaying bells as if to grant their requests.
In whose city the elephants, reflected in the streets paved with jewels, shine like the peaks of mountains on the shore that have descended below to assist the lord of serpents. (1.8)
The golden statues displayed within the palace cages,
brought from the cities of his vanquished enemies, enhance the splendor of the city deities who have been overwhelmed by his power upon the earth.
Having ascended palaces that reach the very path of the clouds, even on days darkened by the rains,
women separated from their lovers dwell there, ignorant of the thundering of wealth.
There, the dwellings— with their exceedingly long golden flagstaffs raised up like arms—
seemed to steal away the splendor of the abodes in the city of Indra, as if out of envy.
When the women, taking with their hands a digit of the moon that clings near the palace,
place it upon their own tresses, they emulate the splendor of Ambikā.

The pavilions, scorched by the intense heat of the summer, seemed to savor the moon with its nectar-like essence through the fluttering hem of their banner-crests, as if tasting the orb of the cool-rayed one itself.
And when the deer, agitated by fear upon seeing the lion-emblem on the banner of the shrine, flees elsewhere,
the moon there attains a resemblance to the faces of the full-hipped women, as if they were lotuses.
In the moon-chambers of the womenfolk who are spreading out their playful ornaments,
the full orb of the nectar-rayed moon, appearing before them at night, serves as a mirror.
Where the spreading channels of light from the gateways made of sapphire gems momentarily cast a suspicion of a dark spot upon the orb of the sun, even as it dwells in their proximity.
There, the rivers— with pleasure-mountains situated on their banks reflected within their clear waters—
assume the splendor of the celestial Ganges, whose divine elephants have sunk beneath the heat of their rut.
Where the sky, by the high and low, surging rays of dwellings fashioned from jewels,
shines as if arrayed with Indra’s rainbows even at the end of the monsoon.
The women belonging to him, who have commenced their play in palatial towers made of gold,
eclipse the splendor of the celestial nymphs sporting upon the peaks of Mount Sumeru.
Where the spreading growths of the blossoming power of crystal-studded dwellings seem to become the momentary chowries upon the ears of the green horses standing nearby.
With its currents dappled by the spreading rays from the jeweled archways,
the great celestial river shines in the midst of the sky as if its interior were mottled by the waters of the Yamunā.
In that city, the sea-monsters of the celestial river, together with the fish-emblems raised upon the palace rooftops and trembling in the wind,
furiously contend with them as if perceiving them to be rivals.
There, the fatigue from amorous play of the graceful women who have taken refuge upon cloud-scraping palaces is dispelled by a gentle breeze that partakes in the sport of the Mandākinī’s waves.

In that city, during the nights, the moon— possessing all its digits and accompanied by nectar— seems to smear the surfaces of the pleasure-houses with its sprout-like rays using ambrosia as its pigment.

Where, upon floors inlaid with sapphire stones, the swans strive to peck with their beaks at the first crescent of the moon— its reflection having entered therein— mistaking it for a fragment of lotus stalk.
Seeing the mass of smoke rising from the house, appearing like a sudden, fierce Rāhu, the Lord of Days (the Sun) seems to hide himself out of fear within the forests of clouds.
The curved splendors of the excellent women reflected upon the crystal surfaces create the illusion that they are blooming lotuses in the waters of the celestial river.
Unable to pass beyond this *sāla* tree that mocks the horizon,
the Lord of Light traverses the earth at its side under the guise of its northern and southern hemispheres.
With its waves, manifested by the agitation of the wind, leaping over the shores,
the moat seems to exert itself as if to conquer the ocean, the lord of jars.
The white silk banners and victory standards atop its palaces, mingled with the incense of black aloe-wood,
shine like the rows of waves of the celestial river Ganges broken by surging billows.
There was a king there, honored and of the Śākya lineage, who possessed the eternal royal fortune;
his conduct was purified by the acquisition of wealth through adherence to dharma, and he was named Śuddhodana, whose name was true to its meaning.
The all-pervading hero, having made the very fire of his majesty a clear witness to the marriage,
wedded the Fortune of the enemy kings by means of the falling water from the edge of his sword.
He who, having first performed his great consecration with the streams of flowing ichor from the temples of rutting elephants,
subsequently offered worship to the deity of battle with the lotus-hearts of his enemies.
In his hand shone a sword with its blade adorned by the letters of horripilation,
like a royal edict sent by Yama himself to summon his enemies.
That sword named Candrahāsa, which surpassed the majesty of all kings who had been subdued and which completely drank up the waters of the enemy's rivers,
brought forth joy to the world upon its appearance, just as the sage Agastya did with his rising.

Like a cloud bearing a rainbow, he who was advancing against the army— abundant with the forces of hostile kings and filled with agitated royal swans— caused it to dance with the leaping of headless trunks.

With their limbs adorned by garlands of the entrails of brave warriors, the Piśācas took up the trunks of elephants as if they were horns and engaged in the sport of mutual splashing within the rivers of their enemies' blood.
The dense, cloud-dark sapphire cloud, established as if it were a vessel for collecting the lamp-ointment of the majesty of that lineage praised by his bride, shone forth.
When the atmosphere was completely filled by his glories, which bore the weight of the entire universe within them,
there was no room for the fame of other kings to spread, as if it were obstructed by those very glories.
If his fame, bright as the moon, had not served as a cooling remedy,
how could this world have endured his unbearable fire of majesty?
While he firmly supported the circle of the earth with his arm, which bore the weight like that of the lord of serpents,
the variegated jeweled bracelets fell from the vine-like arms of the wives of his enemies.
Relying upon that most noble one who was compassionate, the supplicants sought no other;
for having reached the ocean, the bearer of waters, would the clouds ever desire another pond? // 1.42 //
In that palace, which was exceedingly cooled by the flow of fragrant oils from the garlands adorning his shoulders,
the Goddess of Fortune sported, having cast off her garments as if distressed by the fever of the external heat.
During his consecration, by means of the waters brought from the Ganges and other sacred fords and poured by his ministers,
you simultaneously extinguished the power of the fire of your enemies' majesty along with the fever in the hearts of men.

Having approached that mountain-like king— who was golden-hued, worthy of being served by the virtuous, lofty, the peerless abode of the True Dharma, and like Mount Meru— the caravan of the jewels of the six royal qualities shone forth.
Elsewhere, Karna—who was unattached to hearing the heroic deeds of the wise—became engrossed in this;
for does the one who knows flavors ever take pleasure in another taste after casting aside the essence of nectar? // 1.46 //
Thousands of other kings were likewise pacified by him alone; thus the earth became possessed of excellent sovereignty.
Indeed, the ocean, though a source of many jewels, became known as the "Treasury of Jewels" (ratnākara) only because of the Kaustubha gem.
While the nectar-consuming gods were being incessantly summoned by that great-souled one for sacrifices,
the Pārijāta tree grew up as an ornament surpassing even the capital of the sovereign of the gods.
Even today, Mount Meru seems to melt with joy upon hearing his heroic deeds being sung by celestial nymphs standing on its slopes, under the guise of the water flowing from its streams.

While that king was showering down a rain of gifts, not a single person remained with unfulfilled desires. When a great cloud pours down in a continuous stream, is there any pond on earth that does not reach its full capacity? // 1.50 //
Like the river of the ocean, like the lotus-stalk of the sun, like the crescent of the moon, like Lakṣmī of Viṣṇu, or like lightning of a rain-cloud, he had a queen named Māyā. (1.51)
Her pair of lotus-feet, possessing a luster like the interior of a young sprout,
bore upon them her full-moon nails, which acted as blossoming flowers for the creeper-like tresses of her beautiful attendants.
The radiance of the jewels on the nails of that lady, who regarded her husband as a deity,
expanded so brightly that it caused apprehension in the moonlight— herself a refugee from the fear of Rahu.
There was nothing superior to, nor even equal to, the beauty of those two shanks, which possessed such lovely luster and displayed a tenderness through their most wonderful configuration.
Those beautiful elephant-kings with two tusks, and those noble varieties of plantain trees—
they are but droplets in the ocean of beauty expanding from her two shanks.
The lawful wife of the king, her heavy hips encircled by a girdle and bracelets of rubies,
was like the earth— whose womb contains the jewels of the ocean— whose sandy shores are embraced by the shore-line.
The navel-cavity of the girl with arched brows appeared as beautiful as a whirlpool in an ocean of wine;
it seemed like the place where the mountain-like breasts had been hollowed out by the cascades of the liquid flowing from their loveliness.

Upon her body-field, which was rich with the grain of the bodiless god of love, three folds shone like a triple irrigation channel prepared by the plowman of youth to drench it with the waters flowing from the overflow of her beauty.
His birth-house, the sign of poverty, was devoid of the threefold strength of the ascendant;
it shone like the sky embraced by the flowing streams of the celestial Ganges.
The fresh line of hair, dark as the *tāla* tree, shone upon that lotus-eyed maiden like a column of portentous smoke rising to announce the destruction of her childhood state.
As the delicate-limbed maiden was mentally practicing the art of archery with the flower-weaponed god,
the slender line of hair upon her body appeared like a revered bowstring reflected externally upon the surface of her mirror-like form.
As she yawned, her youthful breast-mound overstepped its boundary;
having completely occupied its own space, it remained with only the waistband as its remnant.

The left-eyed maiden shone like a lotus stalk from the pleasure-pool of her graceful movements, a flash of lightning from the cloud-banks of her youth, an auspicious garland for the god of love, and his very arm.
Bearing her neck, which was beautiful with a string of pearls suspended upon it,
she shone intensely like a wave of the ocean, radiant with a conch shell made lovely by a cluster of spumed pearls.

Desiring to create a face like the moon that would have no rival on earth, the Grandfather surely fashioned the lotus with its scent already taken away, and the orb of the moon with its internal stain.
Neither the sprouts of trees, due to their flickering tenderness, nor the corals of the ocean, due to their fixed hardness,
were ever mentioned in comparison to her bimba-like lips, O lotus-eyed one.
The luster of the bimba-fruit lips of that large-eyed woman, scattered with the playfulness of her smile,
shone like the twilight of the bandhūka flower, its appearance variegated by the light of the moon.

The nose of the girl in her fresh youth shone like a great conduit for the overflowing beauty of the crescent moon of her exceedingly lovely forehead, and as the boundary line between the rivers of her two eyes.
Her cheek, with its decorative leaf-patterns fashioned from musk and possessing the splendor of the lunar orb,
stood surpassing the beauty of a mirror whose interior was soiled by the spray of ocean winds.
There was a great distinction between her lotus-eye and the blue water-lily:
the former was the unfailing weapon of the flower-armed god, while the latter had withered away under the heat of ascetic penances.
Defeated even now by her broad eye, which is full of grace,
the young fawns continue to dwell in forest caves as if out of shame.

Her face shone like a lotus flanked by two creeper-like eyebrows— eyebrows that were ripples upon the ocean of her good fortune and branches of the wish-fulfilling tree of her youth, appearing as if accompanied by swarms of bees.
The line upon the forehead of the lotus-eyed one, adorned with beautiful curls,
shone like a victory banner for the God of Love, displaying a row of dots and syllables that seemed to reveal her name.
Her face, enchanting with its two darting glances,
attained a likeness to a lotus in which a pair of pāṭhīna fish were swimming and turning within.
With the luster of yellow orpiment and fair skin, her mass of hair dark as a bee,
she shone like a lamp of auspiciousness at dawn— its upper part greyed by rising smoke— bringing honor to the world.
She alone obtained from her husband that supreme half-seat which could not be attained by any other.
What other women deserve to abandon the fortune that dwells upon the chest of Madhusūdana?
The lord of the earth, desiring a son by that queen who was radiant with praiseworthy virtues,
became intent upon propitiating the deities with offerings such as lamps and incense.
Today, for the sake of a son, he muttered mantras at sacred bathing places, distributed gifts, practiced austerities,
listened to the Dharma, and attended upon virtuous people, together with his lawful wife.
Thus, even as a very long time passed by his merits,
the lord of kings did not obtain a jewel of a son;
yet that longing continued to grow, for the effort of men does not cease until the accomplishment of their goal.
Thus ends the first canto in the great poem titled *Padyacūḍāmaṇi*, the life of Siddhārtha, composed by the master Buddhaghoṣa.
The Second Chapter: The Departure of the Gods to the Tuṣita City.
In the meantime, a portent appeared in the world; seeing that marvel, the hosts of immortals assembled together.
Thinking, "This is the occasion for you to attain omniscience," they went to the city named Tuṣita, the abode of the Teacher of the Gods.
The sky was overspread by the splashing spray of the expanding masses of light from the lofty sapphire palaces;
and near the moon-stones, the shadows cast by the flickering glances of sporting fawn-eyed maidens rose and fell.
The sprouts of light from the ivory balconies of the palace were being licked by the hem of the tongue-like girdle of Līlācakora;
the radiance of the garlands of worship was multiplied by the long, continuous rows of rays from the jeweled archways extending obliquely.
The tinkling sound of the bowstring on the curved bow of the five-arrowed god caused the eyes of the travelers to roll with agitation;
meanwhile, the streets were muddied by the waters of the surging river-like flow of rut from the temples of the elephants of the quarters, blinded by pride.
The radiance from the bodies of the lotus-eyed women, whose eyes were like four-petaled lotuses with a thousand rays, rekindled the rows of lamps;
while the banners raised high upon the palace rooftops, adorned with Chinese silks, served as veils for the women of the quarters.
There, the pleasure-mountains were fashioned by the swelling breasts of groups of women who were bending down to gather flowers;
and the waters of the lakes were rendered superfluous by the streams of nectar-pools dripping from the mango buds.
It possessed the beauty of Indra’s bow, accumulated by the movement of the luster of the nine gems atop its pleasure-pavilion;
it put an end to all talk of poverty through the presence of Mandāra, Kalpa, Haricandana, Pārijāta, and Santāna trees.
There, the hosts of gods beheld him seated upon a lion-throne set with slabs of various jewels,
radiant with many colors from diverse minerals, like the king of beasts on a ridge of Mount Meru.
Nearby stood a venerable white auspicious parasol, fixed upon the ridge of his ruby crown,
rivaling the beauty of the eastern mountain when its lofty jeweled peaks reflect the full moon.
With sacrifices spreading out from all sides toward the sacrificial ground— which was fashioned like a stone slab in a newly cleared forest clearing—
he seemed to be distributing portions of the nectar of his own splendor as an adornment for the faces and wide eyes of the quarters of the sky.
With side-glances that were long and wandered through the waters of the surging tide of his vast ocean of compassion,
he seemed to be creating rows of pleasure-lotuses for the royal fortune of the Lord of the Immortals within the very faces of the quarters.
With exceedingly serene and joyful smiles spreading through the hollows and caves of the sky,
he seemed to be creating an eternal realm of moonlight in order to kindle the ocean of the waters of his own fame.
Together with his circle of friends, who were standing nearby and graced by natural devotion, resembling his own image,
he seemed to be pouring out an inner passion that was throbbing within him, as it was made visible by the glow of his coral-red lips during their conversation.
His gaze was blurred by tears of joy, the lines of his cheeks were adorned with rising thrills of horripilation,
and he listened as the company of actors sang before him of his own noble deeds.
With streams of nectar falling from the clusters of blossoms used as ear-ornaments by the celestial nymphs,
he seemed to perform the grand ceremony of the consecration of a hero for his two arms of noble prowess.

His cheeks were made beautiful by a pair of auspicious earrings fashioned from red and white gems, which— resembling the rising mountain of his lofty pair of arms and the sun born of his splendor, as well as the moonlight of his fame— aroused the suspicion that they were actually the moon and the sun.
With a garland fashioned from mandāra flower buds hanging from the middle of his venerable arms,
he seemed to display the descent of the power of loving-kindness through the stream of red juice flowing from the opening of his throat-vein.

He bore two arms like branches, which, with their rising rosy glow, were delightful to the mind; and by the nets of rays from the sprouts of loosened jeweled bracelets, they seemed as if covered by the young shoots of the splendor of his own heroic majesty breaking forth.
With his limbs smeared with thick paste of yellow sandalwood and marked within by intricate patterns of saffron,
he appeared as if displaying the state of Jīmūtavāhana, whose body had been mangled by the beak of the king of birds.

With the staff-like rays of light from various kinds of jewel-ornaments spreading everywhere throughout the circle of the quarters, he seemed to be instructing them in the duty of manifesting supernatural powers— a sign of the future majesty of the state of enlightenment.

From that moment on, he seemed to practice the art of wearing the saffron robe— the very seal of the state of a sage situated above [the world]— as evidenced by the radiance of his ornaments, which fell like the crimson glow of lotuses blooming all around him down to his lotus-like feet.
With his heart-stealing chest-panels, which served as jeweled finials for the white balconies of the palace,
he possessed the splendor of the enemy of Kaiṭabha— the Lord of the Ocean himself— who dwells visibly upon his breast.
He appeared like a king of elephants, with his lotus-like trunk caressed by red lotuses from which nectar was incessantly dripping,
and with his lotus-eyes crimson as if blood were gushing forth from them at that very moment after being torn open.

Lured by the pervasive fragrance of the sandalwood ointment, the dark masses of impurity on all sides were drawing near; he, as it were, drove them away in every direction with that very scent, like a dense mass of inner darkness caused by ignorance.
With streams of nectar-like luster from his wondrously compact body— spreading forth from the faces of all directions and worthy of universal acclaim—
he seemed to drench the assembly of the king of the gods standing nearby, who was distressed by the heat of his own majesty.
The entire circle of directions was made resonant by the cries of the female peacocks, who were startled by the sound of bracelets slipping from their arms due to the light;
and a multitude of white chowries was being waved nearby by the courtesans of the celestial city.
With his chest encircled by a beautiful necklace of shimmering pearls that resembled a garland of stars, he appeared like the sky itself;
thus, he made the pride of the slopes of the celestial mountain seem like the embrace of a wave from the ocean of the heavens.

He was touching with his right foot a wondrous footstool fashioned from the patterns of unbreakable ruby, shaped like a lotus, which shone like the treasure-lord Padmanidhi bowed down by the power of his generosity.
With the rays of light emerging from his reddened toes— which steal away the splendor of fresh red lac—
he seemed to be showering down a spreading dawn-sunlight to awaken the lotus-faces of the gods who were bowing before him.
With the fresh mass of light from the network of rays from his toenails— resembling the bud-like hands of the Lord of the Stars—
the lotus-navelled one appeared as if his lotus-feet were beautiful with streams of nectar flowing like celestial rivers.

"Is this the time for the protection of people suffering from the terrible torments of saṃsāra, or not?"—as if desiring to descend for a moment out of such a desire to know, he appeared with the likeness of a reflection upon the surface of the ruby-paved floor. (2.31)

Having beheld the Teacher of the Three Worlds, the gods bowed their heads, bending low from afar like the *pārijāta* tree in the Tuṣita abode; and as he moved along, transcending the range of words, they began to honor him with hymns of praise.

O Lord of the Gods, protect us with your side-long glances— those great conduits for the overflowing stream of compassion that expands within the state of beholding the wretched, and which act as whisperers in the ears of the blossoming lotuses of our eyes. 2.33.

O you whose slender body is entwined with the sprouts of the waves of the milk-ocean, which bears the beauty of rising at your own will; O crest-ornament of the deities of the Tuṣita abode, salutations to you who are devoted to the vow of supreme compassion! 2.34

Salutations to you, the ocean of virtues, who are filled with supreme bliss by the honor of being invested with the headband of the rank of Chief Queen of Wisdom; you who are devoted to the assembly of discourse that delights in drinking the nectar of the teachings on the highest stage of life. 2.35.

Salutations to you, whose breasts—the wives of loving-kindness—are adorned with makara-designs and leaf-patterns of sandalwood paste; who cause the caves of the horizons to ripple with waves of splendor; and who are the field for the ripening of the fortune of the three worlds. 2.36.

O you who are the ship of Dharma for the ocean of living beings, which is being intensely scorched by the mass of flames from the submarine fire of Māra’s power; O you whose edict is crowned by the guardians of the world; O you whose majesty pervades the quarters; O sole teacher of the world—homage to you! (2.37)
O you whose vast vision is adorned by the surging waves of a continuous flow of unfailing compassion;
O you whose mental activity is rippled by the liquid nectar of meditative absorption;
O God of gods!
Homage to you, the sole seer of the world.
O you who extinguished the digestive fire of hungry rākṣasas with streams of blood flowing from your throat, which was severed without artifice;
O master craftsman who created the drama of liberation;
O delight of the eyes!
O King of Gods!
Homage, homage to you! 2.39

O Blessed One, salutations to you, whose stream of fame is spread across the quarters of the sky by the songs of the wives of the Gandharva kings; who are devoted to the protection of those capable of liberation; and who possess an abundance of fortune that is now ready to bear fruit. 2.40.

Homage to you, who are the leader of the Tuṣita world, whose pure intention is adorned by excellent conduct, and who surpasses the wish-fulfilling tree and the cow of plenty with the splendor of your great, perpetual, and faultless giving. 2.41

Homage to you, whose face is as delightful to the mind as the orb of the full moon; who has cast aside the power of the finest water-vehicles; whose intention is peaceful; who has swallowed the strength of the arms of the fish-bannered god with his fist; and whose intellect is honored by the sages. 2.42.

We bow to you alone, O Varadarāja, whose staff-like arms surpass the trunks of the lordly elephants that adorn the far reaches of the quarters, and whose beautiful lotus-face has blossomed with loveliness. 2.43.
O Hero! You alone are skilled in the act of overthrowing the fish-bannered god who has conquered all the quarters of the sky;
for who else in this world, save a lion, possesses such a steadfast mind as to conquer an elephant that has shattered the peaks of mountains? (2.44)
O you who are a mass of merit for those who have come for refuge, you alone are capable of removing the entire torment of hatred from the worlds;
for who on earth could be able to extinguish a forest fire without a rain-cloud flashing with flickering lightning? // 2.45 //
The three worlds have been robbed by the darkness of delusion; O you of superior merit, you alone are skilled in awakening them.
For who else is able to cause the groves of autumnal lotuses to bloom except for the sun, the friend of the world? (2.46)

O Lord of the radiant ones, you alone are most capable of drying up the flood of craving for living beings; for who in this world, other than the submarine fire at the end of an aeon, would be able to drink up the lord of waters? (2.47)

O Wise One, you alone possess the skill to lead the three worlds to the further shore across the ocean of existence; for who else, aside from you who assumed the form of the deceptive boar, was capable of lifting the earth from the depths of the sea? (2.48)
Having thus heard with reverence the hymn of praise offered by the gods, the Lord of the Tuṣita heaven, his heart filled with joy,
replied to them in words of sweet syllables, deep as the rumbling of a thundercloud.
"O you guardians of the quarters, headed by Purandara, why have you all come here together with such respect?
If there is any task whatsoever desired by you that I must perform, let it be told; enough with this abundance of praise."
With minds full of serene faith, bowing down before him with bodies bent low in humble reverence, they addressed him:
"O God of gods, for the sake of awakening the world..."
"The appropriate occasion for you has arrived. // 2.51 //
Having heard those words never before heard by them, he paused for a moment, intent on reflecting upon Time and other factors;
then, having ascertained all of that, this treasury of virtues, whose heroic deeds are renowned, replied once more to them.
"Having come here as the son of Śuddhodana, I shall surely bring about the awakening to truth for the three worlds;
having previously sought this very goal even with my limbs, wealth, and life-breaths, I have accumulated a store of merit. (2.53)

When he, who was true to his word, intent on the welfare of others, and devoted to the ultimate perfection of the virtues, had thus made his vow, those beings returned as they desired, their minds filled with joy and their bodies covered by a dense thicket of rising horripilation.
Then, after spending only a few days in the third heaven,
that king of the gods brought about a rebirth for himself in the queen of the lord of the earth, who was radiant with various vows.
Thus ends the second canto in the great poem titled *Padyacūḍāmaṇi*, composed by Buddhaghoṣa.
The Third Canto:
The manifestation of the signs of pregnancy, and the dawning of joy for the eyes of the people belonging to the lineage of the Śākya monarchs.
That noble lady, manifesting the signs of pregnancy, brought consolation to the hearts of the virtuous.
As her nipples grew larger and turned dark, the onset of pregnancy became inferable by her friends through the languid gaze of that woman with beautiful eyes. (3.2)
When the Bodhisattva— who was worthy of honor even by the great sages— entered the womb,
the king’s subtle mental state toward him became even more expansive than his affection for his own beloved.
Just as the waist of that queen of noble form grew larger,
so too did the body of her husband— who was emaciated by the grief of childlessness— grow larger.
The tips of her two breasts turned pale along with the face of her rival;
moreover, the face of that woman languid from the weight of her pregnancy became as white as the fame of her husband.

The breast of that woman, its surface darkened by the smoke-like clouds from the fire of his majesty—whose wondrous valor was contained within and whose form caused wonder throughout the three worlds—became dark-faced. (3.6)
The pair of breasts of that woman of faultless limbs— dark at the tips and pale in the remainder—
bore the beauty of the frontal globes of the lord of serpents, marked by the mud left from striking against the riverbank.
The aged women performed various protections with medicinal herbs for their son while he remained in the womb;
that very same protection became the defense for the three worlds of those afflicted by the assault of the god of love.
At an auspicious moment, the king— whose royal splendor was equal to that of Indra— performed for his queen, who bore a heavy burden in her womb,
the rites beginning with the *puṃsavana* in due order, in accordance with his lineage.
At an auspicious moment, like the dawn bringing forth the thousand-rayed sun or the beauty of evening giving birth to the cool-beamed moon,
the lawful wife of the king gave birth to a son who was the sole eye of the world.
In that interval, for the sake of his dwelling, the earth appeared as if it had been offered a gift, being covered with noble, upturned lotuses of five beautiful colors.
With their hundreds of various blossoms emerging on every branch, even the trees themselves seemed to have acquired eyes in order to behold him. (3.12)

Just as our own birth upon this earth was rare, so too was the sprouting of the Buddhas; indeed, for the sake of manifesting them to embodied beings, the sky did not become a mere falsehood even upon the dry land. (3.13)
"Through his instruction, the entire world of living beings will truly attain Nirvana. What need is there for our own brilliant efforts? Even the fires of hell would surely reach Nirvana. (3.14)
Unable, as it were, to endure the treads of that Great-Souled One, which were heavy with the weight of his mountain-like fall, the Earth trembled violently, her bonds of mountains loosened.
Tall as palm trees, with surging currents, they suddenly burst forth from the earth.
For the sake of paying homage to that virtuous soul, those under Śeṣa’s command were like the inhabitants of the serpent world.
All the directions became brightened, as if being smeared by the streams of his fame— which were spread everywhere and white as the foam of the waters of the sky.

As if proclaiming, "He who was born is the sovereign of the earth, the lord of sages and of the worlds," various auspicious musical instruments—conchs, ānakas, mṛdaṅgas, and other varieties of wind and percussion instruments—resounded spontaneously. (3.18)
As if to perform the preparations for the great consecration of the one of great majesty,
all the oceans, having transgressed their shores, surged forward with faces of uplifted waves.
The name "Immovable" was shaken from Meru; the surge of salt water from the ocean faltered;
the designation of the river as "flowing" ceased; and the title of the earth as "unstable" came to an end.
Even without the rainy season, the cloud, with the deep roar of the ocean, poured down rain;
such were the wondrous deeds that occurred when the Kumāra, the foremost of the virtuous, was born.
The mouths of the caves resounded with the noise of many beaten drums,
while the mountains shook as the earth swayed from the whirling dances of those filled with joy.
The ground was starred with pearls from necklaces shattered by mutual pressure, while the entire expanse of the quarters was made radiant by handfuls of *piṣṭātaka* powder thrown about. (3.23)
With their ornaments mutually cast aside and their crest-jewels and diadems fallen away,
the splendor of that great birth festival was like that of the three worlds gathered together in a single abode.
With her son, whose complexion was as rosy as that of a fresh embryo, the mother shone all the more,
like the shore with the young moon when its body is reddened by its first rising light.
By the spreading radiance of his body, which shone like refined gold,
the lamps in the birth-chamber became like the stars at dawn.
Hearing from the people of the inner apartments this most wonderful news of the birth of his son, the lord of men—
his mental faculties overwhelmed by a swoon of joy and bewildered as to what ought to be done— stood motionless.
Having seen no object in the three worlds worthy of such a gift as this,
the exceedingly noble king nevertheless honored him with the gift of all his possessions.
At an auspicious moment, that lord of subjects, with his large eyes steady and wide, beheld the prince lying upon the lap of the queen, like a young swan upon the bank of a river.
As his son tasted the moon of his face with eyes that were unwearying and thirsty,
the flow of tears of joy from the father— whose slender body was bristling with horripilation— was checked.
Having drunk deeply with the cupped hands of his eyes the moon-disk of the suckling’s face—a repository of the nectar of unceasing beauty—the lord of kings attained supreme bliss. (3.31)
Having completed the most magnificent birth-rites and other ceremonies for his son with the help of the family priest,
he bestowed upon him the world-renowned name "Siddhārtha," a title to which no one else was worthy.
The lineage was adorned by him, as the vault of heaven is by a fresh rain-cloud, as the night is by the youthful lord of stars, and as the great forest is by the cub of a lion. (3.33)
Just as the king’s mind became gladdened by his words, whose syllables were indistinct, so it was not even by the songs of singers or by the verbal flourishes of great poets. (3.34)
Her face, naturally fragrant and exceedingly charming, possessed such delicacy that it became the common,
unfading lotus of the beauty of the women within the inner apartments.
Making his mother’s joy swell with the heart-pleasing sounds of jeweled anklets,
the son played upon the jeweled floors, cherishing the conceit that they were reflections of himself.
Together with his companions, the sons of ministers who had attained skill in playing in the dust,
he was like one who had been made fit by practice to roam at will upon the battlefields of the future.
That prince, playing with the lion cubs within the inner apartments,
for a long time acted as if he were providing instruction to them in their own most marvelous prowess.
The prince, unable to endure their royal title, struck with his foot those royal swans of the house who were crying out in joy at the sound of the jeweled anklets following him.
With his head shaken by the blows of his goad-like claws, the beauty of his trumpeting enhanced by the roar from his mouth, and with streaks of ichor flowing as auspicious signs,
the young elephant displayed the grace of a rutting tusker.

Radiant with the brilliance of a blooming garland of campaka flowers, and bringing light to the world of the living, that boy, like a kindled lamp, dispelled the darkness of grief for his parents. (3.41)

Having performed the investiture with the sacred thread and having passed beyond childhood, the lord of the earth entrusted that most excellent youth into the hands of his teachers for the thorough study of all branches of knowledge. (3.42)
Being instructed by the foremost of teachers, he— by virtue of his intelligence— mastered all the sciences and all the arts in a short time, just as a rain-cloud draws water from the ocean.

Having found in the Prince a mind that was unique and peerless, the sciences shone forth with even greater brilliance, just as the garlands of rays from the Lord of Stars shine upon the expanse of the sky made clear by autumn. (3.44)
By him, who exceedingly gladdened the minds of the people and instantly dispelled the darkness,
the Śākya lineage blossomed forth like the great ocean at the rising of the moon.
Like the radiance of the sun, like the brilliance of a sage, like the flame of a lamp, like the compassion of a virtuous man,
like the moonlight of the moon, and like the nectar of the ocean— so did the splendor of his new youth arise.
As if sharpened on the whetstone of his exceptional youth by the God of Love,
his limbs became clearly manifest with their characteristic marks and well-defined joints.
His pair of feet, possessing innate beauty and marked with a thousand spokes and the sign of the wheel, surely mocked the fresh groves of lotuses with the moonlight of his toenail radiance. (3.48)
The prince, whose slender waist was beautiful with the ornament of the three folds,
appeared like Mount Mandara encircled by the coils of Vāsuki, its middle shimmering with the celestial streaks [of light].
Along with all his virtues, the prince’s rounded hips attained fullness;
and along with all his faults, his waist became slender. (3.50)
The lake of his navel, with its dark stalk of the line of body hair as its reed,
appeared like a pit dug by the god of love desiring to plant it there.

The chest of that virtuous man, as broad as a slab from the Vindhya mountains, became like a space provided without restraint for the Goddess of Fortune, who had been dwelling uncomfortably within a lotus.

Although that heroic son of a protector of the earth possessed door-panels as solid as adamant, living beings made door-panels for their dwellings for the sake of ornamentation, and not for the sake of protection. (3.53)
The arm of that king, skilled in protecting his subjects, was as long as the coils of the lord of serpents;
it was beyond the reach of rival monarchs and served as a bolt for the protection of the three worlds.
With its graceful contours made exceedingly clear by distinct lines,
that neck shone as if marked with the impressions of armlets, as if firmly embraced by the splendor of beauty.
There was a great distinction between that lotus-face of his while he was still an infant and a great blue lotus:
the former bore a steady radiance, whereas the latter bore a beauty naturally fickle. (3.56)
The well-spoken word of the Exalted One, dwelling in his mouth, resounded like the tinkling of anklets;
the moonlight of his smile was like the luster of his nails, and the row of his teeth was like a rosary of pearls. (3.57)

The beauty of the lotus-like splendor of her face was a jeweled mirror; the surface of her cheeks was the charm of a gem-studded mirror; her dangling ear-ornaments were a pleasure-swing; and her eye was a pond for amorous play. (3.58)
The creeper-like brow of him whose form was so charming, with its two ends kissed by the rays of the stars,
was like the playful bow of Māra, having conquered him and been brought under his own control, with the bee-like pupils fixed as its string.
His lotus-face, radiant with light and beautiful with a circle of serene ūrṇā-hair,
extensively displayed the splendor of the crescent moon within it and the brilliance of the rising sun.
The prince’s forehead, beautiful with its tuft of hair,
shone intensely like the slope of a mountain peak on Mount Meru, where the sprouts of elephant tusks lie hidden after being broken by the work of a boar.
Even without cosmetic ointment, without armlets, without a crest-jewel, and even without a garland,
his body was revealed to be most enchanting by virtue of its fresh youth.

Bringing joy to the deer-eyed women, never before directed toward other men, and serving as a natural ornament for the entire form of her body, that collective beauty of hers had now come forth. (3.63)

The king, whose own nature was like that of the Lord of the Gods, performed the consecration for the office of crown prince upon his son— whose arms were capable of supporting the circle of the entire earth—
with waters from sacred bathing places filled in jeweled jars and purified by mantras.
Thus ends the third canto in the great poem named *Padyacūḍāmaṇi*, composed by Buddhaghoṣa.
The Fourth Canto: The Proposal for Prince Siddhārtha’s Marriage.
Then the king, desiring to have the hand-grasping ceremony performed for the prince, the upholder of his lineage, [proceeded].
"Who on earth is the maiden worthy of him? he wondered, gathered with his kinsmen.
In the meantime, the Koliya ruler sent him a message on a letter, saying: "I shall give my daughter, a jewel-lamp of my lineage, to your son in every respect."
Having heard the news from the messenger’s mouth, the lord of the earth was exceedingly pleased in mind;
he dispatched a further message to him, saying, "Let it be prepared by you in that very same manner."
"So be it," he replied, and accepting the letter of message from him with surging joy,
he proceeded to arrange a most magnificent festival for the maiden’s marriage consecration.
It was adorned with sky-scraping rows of banners, beautified by suspended canopies of silk,
marked by lofty triumphal arches bearing the sign of Indra’s bow, and featured full vases placed within.
The inner apartments of the lord of the earth became delightful with strewn sands of pearls, scattered with offerings of various flowers,
and occupied with preparations for the wedding.
Those beautiful women respectfully bathed her, whose limbs were anointed with scented oil and whose body was rubbed with fragrant myrobalan, with clouds of water poured from jeweled jars.
At the conclusion of her bath, the princess, having discarded her garment wet with the weight of water,
put on a most beautiful silk robe, like an autumn night assuming the moonlight.
Then, having seated the princess in the middle of a courtyard strewn with fresh blossoms, her friends,
who were highly skilled, adorned her with various kinds of ornaments.
The loosened hair-braid of the tremulous-eyed woman, in which full-blown jasmine flowers were tucked within,
spread the beauty of a dense cluster of darkness variegated by a multitude of stars.
Her lotus-face shone with excellent locks of hair whose tips were curled,
appearing as if they were bees settling there out of greed for the abundance of its fragrance.

The marriage-consecration mark, fashioned with vermilion by the princess of the king, shone brightly like the rising sun, the very form of the majesty of the God of Love who had attained sovereignty. (4.12)
The barley sprouts resting upon the ears of the lotus-eyed maiden shone with extraordinary brilliance,
like the burgeoning shoots of fame belonging to the flower-armed god who conquers the three worlds.
Her cheek, its decorative leaf-patterns fashioned from musk and possessing the splendor of the lunar orb,
stood surpassing the beauty of a mirror whose interior was soiled by the winds from the clouds.
The eye of the fish-eyed maiden, beautiful with its applied black collyrium,
followed the splendor of the arrow of the Bodiless One, as if smeared with the mud of most virulent *hālāhala* poison.
The application of lac-paste, though prepared for her lovely lip—which possessed a unique, peerless rosy hue—did not produce a beauty such as had never been seen before. (4.16)
Adorned with two pearl earrings, the face of the lotus-eyed woman, with its gentle smile,
surpassed an autumnal red lotus that has white lotus buds situated on either side.
Bearing a neck adorned with a visible string of pearls, she shone intensely,
like a wave of the ocean radiant with a conch shell beautiful with a cluster of spewed pearls.
Her body, anointed with sandalwood paste and variegated with streaks of fragrant black aloe-wood,
enhanced the beauty of that divine river whose waters were mottled by the Yamunā.

The pair of breasts of that woman of faultless limbs, with its shimmering necklace of smooth pearls, bore the beauty of the peak of the sunset mountain, lovely with its scattered clusters of stars. (4.20)

Adorned in her middle by three sacrificial offerings (*balis*), the slender girl, bearing the weight of her swaying breasts, shone like a lotus pond filled with water-weeds—she who was rippling and whose limbs were covered in a network of spray, resembling the *cakravāka* birds. (4.21)
The king’s daughter, her heavy hips adorned with girdles and bracelets of rubies,
was like the earth itself— whose shores are embraced by the ocean, the womb of jewels, and its sandy banks.

As she grew, the fresh line of hair upon her shone like a garland of blue lotuses suspended for support from the mountain of her high breasts, as if for the sake of providing a foothold for the source of erotic passion.
Adorned with ornaments fashioned from priceless gold,
the fair-limbed girl shone like a moving campaka creeper, radiant with its fresh blossoms.
The pair of tender feet of the long-eyed maiden, their passion intensified by the clinging of red lac,
surpassed the beauty of a lotus stalk, which is only visible through its special contact with the rays of the morning sun.
Desiring to behold her perpetual beauty, she held up a crystal mirror;
she shone like the eastern quarter of Indra’s domain when it touches the orb of the full moon.

Immediately thereafter, the kinsmen bound their curious gaze not only upon the lotus-hand of the priest, whose slender body was as graceful as a stalk and whose desires were fulfilled, but also upon her own lotus-heart.
Having thus completed the preparations for the maiden's wedding adornment,
the curious King of Kauli stood waiting, watching for the arrival of the bridegroom.
Then, in his own home, the son of the supreme king—having bathed, anointed himself, and put on freshly washed garments—donned the wedding ornaments that bring joy to the eyes of the world. (4.29)
With his upper garment of fine linen interwoven with golden threads,
that prince shone like the expanse of the sky covered by an autumn cloud streaked with lightning.
With a string of pearls hanging from his broad chest,
the prince shone like a golden mountain with a glittering streak of shadow along its slope.
With a serene and profound form, the prince, adorned with earrings made of coral and pearls like the orbs of the fierce-rayed sun and the moon, appeared like Mount Meru.
Wet with yellow sandalwood paste, the excellent one shone like the mountain of sunrise copper-red with the morning glow;
like an elephant streaked with lines of mineral dust, or like the moon thickened by the light of twilight.
The reflection of the body of a young man adorned with loosened jeweled ornaments, appearing in the mirror-like orb of the sun,
enhanced the splendor of that ancient being.
The natural radiance of the body of that prince was itself his ornament;
indeed, his other ornaments were merely the insignia of sovereignty, such as those made of rubies.
Having mounted his state elephant, which was worthy of a wedding procession and whose beauty was enhanced by the lifting of the sun-shade and the waving of yak-tail fans,
the prince went to the house of his kinsmen.
When he had arrived, the sovereign of the Koliyas, the lord of the earth, himself approached on foot that lamp of the Śākya clan from afar and led him to the wedding pavilion.
The wise one beheld there the daughter of the protector of the earth, whose face was like the king of stars,
shining like the daughter of the ocean with a play-lotus held in her hand.
As the prince gazed longingly at the maiden, whose limbs surpassed the splendor of the moon,
the ocean of his joy surged far beyond its bounds.
Having performed all that which is to be done there by those devoted wives, the prince,
together with her whose eyes were as broad as lotus petals, entered the midst of the sacrificial altar where the matted locks had been placed.
Before that sacrificial fire, which blazed intensely with its flames upward due to the oblations,
the family priest, whose mind was fixed on the ritual procedures, united the bride and the bridegroom.
The prince’s slender body was covered by bristling hairs standing on end;
the filaments falling from his garland worn across the shoulder served as a protection for that heap of jewels of virtue.
The fingers of the Koliya maiden became moist with emerging drops of perspiration;
these served as a pretext for the spray of water from the wedding procession of the large-eyed girl.
Constantly turning toward him out of longing for his light and turning away again out of modesty,
the extensions of their sidelong glances then experienced the beauty of a swinging motion.
Like the playful whirling of a water-vortex in a vessel accustomed to containing water,
the bridegroom performed the circumambulation of the fire together with the fair-eyed maiden.
Beholding the maiden and the prince of lovely form— whom he had never seen before— the sacrificial fire,
under the guise of the flickering of its circumambulatory flames, seemed to perform a nod of the head in praise.
Directed by her teacher, that noble lady offered an oblation of parched grain into the fire,
like a creeper shaken by the wind casting its flowers upon a mango tree with its fresh sprouts already formed.
The column of smoke rising from the fire that had caught the lotus of her mouth assumed the graceful appearance of the unfading dark blue lotus-stalk of the lotus-eyed woman.
Therefore, as her face was brightened by the grasping of that [smoke],
a rising line of fresh smoke was seen for a moment moving across it like a swarm of bees upon a lotus.
The wreath of auspicious smoke scattered all around her lotus-like face bore the manifest beauty of a halo,
as if she were another moon mistaken for the [true] nectar-rayed one.
The auspicious trail of smoke from the wedding fire, which had enveloped the lotus-face of the fair-eyed maiden,
bore the beauty of a momentary veil made of dark blue silk.

From inhaling the smoke, the lotus-face of the deer-eyed woman became such that her eyes were narrowed by the fumes of black collyrium, the decorative paintings on her cheeks were marred by tears of grief, and the blue lotuses upon her ears turned pale.
Having thus received the hand-pressing (marriage) in due order, the prince bowed together with her to his parents-in-law;
they too, expressing their approval, honored him with blessings that increased his prosperity.
Having honored all his other circles of kinsmen as well, the prince, accompanied by his wife, departed from there and proceeded toward the circumambulation of his own royal capital. (4.54)
At that moment, in every palace, among the women of Kapila who were wholly intent on gazing at the prince, amorous gestures taught by the God of Love broke forth.
For instance, one woman, holding a garland of white water-lilies with her bud-like hand, hurried along the path of the palace stairs as if to choose a husband for herself. (4.56)
Thinking as if "lest this [beauty] become an obstruction to my eye which is motionless in gazing upon it," a certain long-eyed woman quickly removed her black collyrium and hastened to the window.
Thinking, "If my limbs are concealed by ornaments, he will not perceive their natural luster," a certain woman, as if preparing her own attire, suddenly approached a window.

"If I were to place this blooming, fragrant [lotus] upon her ear-pendant, the bee would surely torment her"— disregarding this thought, I believe some woman departed with the lotus from her ear, leaving it behind like a snare.
"Born from the joy of beholding his face, the bristling of the hair on my breast alone is my ornament"—
as if saying this, one woman discarded her leaf-patterned garment and approached the window.
As if restraining her by suggesting that a journey for a devoted wife to see another man is improper,
the girdle slipping from the orb of a certain woman's hips caught upon her foot.
A certain woman, without having offered a single-string necklace to her neck with her lotus-hand,
set out in haste, as if to present it to him as an offering.
With those women intent on gazing at him, the continuous stretches of the palace rooftops became like the encampment of the army of the fish-bannered god who seeks to conquer the world.
In every street, the tremulous side-glances of the playful women fell upon him,
like the flower-arrows of the Flower-bannered God whose slender body was concealed by the lattice-windows of the palaces.
The large-eyed women, never satiated, gazed at him with sidelong glances that reached to their ears; unable to move from one limb to another, they remained fixed upon his every part. 4.65.
With their eyes like lotuses, fixed in wonder and unblinking, the prince appeared as if he were the thousand-eyed Indra himself, his form poured out across every limb of those women.
Wherever on the prince’s body the eyes of the women were directed,
right there they became as if permeated and adhered by the exudation of his loveliness.
To those women who were distressed with the appearance of young maidens, their eyes wide and motionless,
he entered each one’s inner heart as if desiring to dispel the suffering born of love.

At that moment, one woman, her slender body covered in horripilation, inhaled with eyes closed in bliss a lotus of grace held in her hand, which was indistinguishable from his own lotus-like face. (4.69)
One woman, it is said, desiring to mutter a mantra taught by Kāma for the purpose of attracting him— which she had mastered—
gently twirled her string of pearls with her hand as if it were a rosary of beads.
With a fingernail as rosy as the beak of a parrot, a certain woman was scratching a fresh *ketaka* petal held in her hand, as if to write a message of love for him.
Holding a tablet for painting and a brush with its tuft in her sprout-like hand,
she stood as if intent on making an effort to draw her own likeness and give it to that suitor.
The vision of a certain woman became, as it were, clouded by the incessant showers of pollen falling from the flower-arrows born of the mind, as her eyes overflowed with rising tears.
The cheek of a certain woman, enchanting with its emerging crop of bristling hair,
shone like an auspicious vessel held by the God of Love upon entering her heart, its sprouts already taken root.
One woman, her upper garment slipping, trembled as if being shaken by the feathers of the flock of geese belonging to Kāma, who had drawn his bowstring back to his ear.
Interspersed with rising sprays of drops of nectar-like Dharma,
she shone like a certain vine of the bow of Smara, firmly drawn and budding with sprouts of emitted pearls.
As he entered the gateway of the mind, some woman, as if her body were mottled by the scattered clouds of pollen from the trees of the God of Love, fell into a state of paleness.

What incalculable merit must this Bimbā have performed in previous births to obtain as her husband this prince, the preeminent leader of his lineage and mountain, endowed with such supreme beauty? (4.78)
The Creator first fashioned the storehouse of nectar, the orb of the cool-rayed moon, and the lotuses— the celestial chariots of Lakṣmī— solely for the purpose of crafting his face.
Having repeatedly gathered the very essence of beauty from the three worlds at the time of his creation, the Lotus-born One likely fashioned him as the crown prince.
Why did Viriñca, the knower of the three worlds, not create ten thousand eyes for us to behold this youth, whose arms are long as a yoke and whose beauty is desired by the three worlds? (4.81)
Through the consumption of the nectar of beauty produced from the orb of the moon of his face, whose eyes do not attain a state of being unblinking in this very life? (4.82)
Hearing these and other words of theirs, so exceedingly noble and pleasing to the ear,
the prince circumambulated the city and entered the inner palace of the king.
Having entered with his head bowed low from afar, making a salutation with his hands joined like a bud,
the lamp of the Śaka dynasty, accompanied by her, paid homage to his father with words of affection.
Having raised up her husband— who was bent low and bewildered— with his two uplifted arms acting as a cage,
the lord of the earth, his slender body covered in horripilation, embraced him with great affection.
Immediately thereafter, the women of his retinue performed the auspicious lustration ceremony for him as he sat upon the noble throne, using camphor lamps placed in golden vessels.

Having thus witnessed the prince— who had performed his marriage, whose fame rested upon the entire universe, and who was girded for the vow of protecting the three worlds— the king, being filled with joy, considered his own lineage to be exceedingly exalted, having humbled the pride of rival dynasties.
Thus ends the fourth canto in the great poem named *Padyacūḍāmaṇi*, composed by Buddhaghoṣa.
The Fifth Canto:
Then three great palaces were built for the prince, whose sovereign lord possessed complete majesty and who was endowed with the splendor of fresh youth.
He caused three incomparable great temples to be built, which were capable of accommodating the observance of seasonal festivals.
In those palaces, the prince, being entertained by the captivating and graceful dances of excellent courtesans distinguished by their various and exquisite arrangements, passed his time in pleasure.
Then the rainy season arrived, capable of quelling the harsh fever of heat upon the earth,
the sovereign instructor in the sequence of graceful dance for the circles of peacocks throughout the entire forest.
Some clouds, dark as glass and driven by the fierce wind,
shone forth like worn-out sloughs being slowly cast off by the black serpent of the sky.
Then, having ascended the pavilion of the monastery together with his bride,
the lotus-eyed one began to describe the end of the summer heat, pointing out the breasts of the fish-eyed women.

O lotus-eyed one, look from here at the clouds that steal away the sight of the ocean’s mass of waters— clouds resembling the reflection of the earth’s orb entered into the mirror of the expansive expanse of the sky. 5.6.

O lady with arched brows, this expanse of the sky is perceived as a vessel filled with fresh fragments of clouds, which, polished by the lamps of blazing lightning— the very splendor of the season— resemble heaps of applied collyrium.

O beloved, as the new clouds appear, the tresses of the quarters shine forth most beautifully, like locks of hair released by one who has returned after a long journey abroad during the rainy season. (5.8)
As the fire born of the sacrificial hearth subsides with the arrival of the end of the heat,
masses of clouds enter the expanse of the sky like surging waves of smoke.
Those very mountains, which in former times— before their wings were clipped— had fled to the ocean out of fear of Indra’s assault,
now seem to rise up once more under the guise of newly emerging clouds.
O fawn-eyed one, the expanse of the sky shines with clouds reflecting streaks of lightning,
like the ocean at the end of an eon with spheres of mud tossed about by creeping coral vines.

Beholding the graceful movements of peacocks named Śikhaṇḍins, who possess the splendor of wondrous dances and utter sweet cries upon the stage of the forest, the rain-cloud seems to offer praise with its thundering, using lightning as its eyes.
Seizing with their beaks the worlds of the lord of serpents, which resemble golden trumpets, the peacocks—
filling the sky with their deep cries and forming circles with their tails arched over their heads— shout aloud.

O lady with eyes like those of a cakora bird, the streaks of lightning shine as if they were lines of gold being rubbed upon the touchstone of the rows of clouds by a goldsmith whose very self is the heat of the forge at the end of the summer.
"Only my body is soiled, but my inner heart is pure"—thus the cloud seems to reveal this to me by parting [the darkness] under the guise of its flickering, shimmering rays. (5.15)
On the mountain peaks along the shore of Bhārī, whose chariot-rims are the ocean and who dwells within the midst of the four great seas,
rows of clouds adorned with clusters of lightning shine like the river Sītā.

O tremulous-eyed one, having conquered the three worlds with its wondrous splendor and its heroism in giving, this cloud creates doubt regarding the raised banners of victory belonging to the lightning flashes. 5.17
O you of restless glance, the lightning flashes gleam like cane-staffs used for clearing away white parasols;
tossed by the dense clouds as they perform the act of threatening those who dwell afar, they appear like the fingers of a hand.
Having playfully taken up the bow of great Indra, made beautiful by the lightning that serves as its string,
the hunter-like rainy season makes the earth devoid of white lotuses with his multitudes of arrows.
The rays of the Indra-blue sapphire shine intensely, possessing the splendor of the crest-jewels vomited by serpents;
they possess the beauty of fragments of gem-stones scattered from the lap of a mountain struck by a fierce downpour.
Upon the surface of fresh green grass, which is as radiant as the belly of the autumnal night sky,
fall the insects that guard the thunderbolt, resembling stars reddened by a dense cluster of knots.
To measure what distance lies between heaven and earth,
the streams from the clouds fall on all sides like measuring-threads being stretched out by the First Creator.

O lady with eyes like those of a cakora bird, this row of clouds, accompanied by a multitude of cranes chirping excessively and bearing conch shells, seems to loudly proclaim the manifest expedition of the god whose bow is sugarcane across the face of every direction.
With their neck-chains of cranes appearing like the coils of serpents and their variegated blankets of rainbows bestowed upon them,
the young cloud-elephants on the mountains bow down, bearing thunderous roars as if for the purpose of striking against the slopes.
Adorned with garlands of campaka flowers flashing like lightning, and crowned with the beautiful rainbows of Indra,
the quarters of the sky seem to be sprinkling one another with the peaks of clouds filled with fresh water.
As the victorious summer, the sovereign of the seasons, plunges into the palace of the sky,
the rainbows of Indra shine most brightly, appearing like festooned archways fastened by clouds.
As the walls of the horizon tremble through the playful lashing of the thunderbolt-tusked elephant,
these onion-hued hailstones fall as if the clusters of stars were being shattered to pieces.
Taking up vast quantities of water from the great ocean along with its streams of milk,
the cloud now scatters upon the earth hailstones that sparkle like heaps of pearls divided once more.
Just as the fire of lightning expands within the circle of clouds with each rain shower, so too does the fire of love surely expand within the hearts of the fawn-eyed travelers. 5.29
The forest glade, blazing with the heat of the summer season, extends its hands of blossoming *kandalī* stalks;
with the heart-stealing cries of peacock calls, it seems to entreat the cloud for the gift of life-giving rain.
Carrying the pollen of the filaments from the flowers in the bowers of the blossoming forest,
these gentle breezes, sprouting forth like new shoots, dispel the exhaustion born of the peacocks' frantic dancing.
Upon the broad path of the sky-king, where clouds wander hither and thither,
drops of water fall slowly on all sides like the spreading dust of trees.
While the circle of clouds was being proclaimed by lightning, making the fresh fire of lightning its witness,
the season— the priest— initiates the festival of grasping hands in the form of waves between the river and the ocean.
In this time, when all prosperity has been fully brought about by means of the elixirs of immortality,
even the entire earth would in every way assume the status of a tutelary deity for women who have no sons.
While the prince, eager with curiosity, was thus extolling his own life-story,
all the clouds vanished into the quarters of the sky as if overcome by shame.

Then the autumn season appeared, in which the complexion of the women of the quarters was as if anointed with saffron, the paths of the aviaries were filled with white-winged birds, and the lotus-beds displayed the blossoming charms of youth.

As if from the sorrow of separation, the clouds became sealed in silence and turned pale— the clouds that are the beloved of lightning, possess the wealth of playful grace, and are the pure-bred mothers of the cranes.
When the arrival of the rains had brought about the destruction of the display of their own qualities by the clouds,
the flocks of swans arose like the joyful smiles of the deer-eyed women of the quarters.
Hearing the clamor of the white-winged birds whose minds were agitated with distress,
the young women who were suffering separation bitterly censured Bhārgava in their hearts.

The entire cave of the direction of Indra was filled by flocks of swans with outspread wings, which resembled circles of foam from the mine of infinite jewels and evoked the illusion of clusters of blossoms from the fame of the Bodiless One (Kāma).

The expanding masses of pollen from the blossoming *saptaparṇa* trees, wafting in all directions with their burgeoning fragrance, created the illusion of being scented powders applied to the faces of the women.
While the elephants, intoxicated with rut, were being urged on and pouring forth a torrential rain of ichor,
the great rivers became filled with exceedingly swollen waters, even though the rainy season had passed.
The Lord of the Arts (the Moon) spread his radiant web of rays intensely across all directions,
eager as it were to form a firm chain of limbs for the beds of night-lotuses who had long been longing for him.
Waving with the loads of moonlight that were their smiles, made white by their exquisite silken garments,
the young women of the quarters appeared as if they had put on veils out of shame at the sight of the Moon, the King of the Twice-born.
The rows of autumnal clouds were mistaken for masses of ash-dust scattered by the wind from the thickets of Tamāla trees, whose forms had been leaped over by forest fires ignited by the sun.
With its spreading autumnal clouds, it mocked the sky strewn with fragments;
and with the breaking of its waves, it emulated the splendor of the salt ocean at the end of an eon, when the waters of the great receptacle of waters had burst forth.
Having first been consecrated by thick showers of rain, and then having their upper garments held back by masses of autumnal clouds,
they anointed their limbs with moonbeams as if with sandalwood paste and took on the appearance of the quarters of the sky adorned with clusters of stars like strings of pearls.
Upon the clouds that had recently bathed the quarters of the sky— which were like beautiful women with the luster of lovely garments—
the droplets of water clinging to their bodies shone forth as stars with exceeding brilliance.
The clusters of night-lily buds, blooming under the caressing rays of the moon,
shone like hosts of stars reflected in the waters of lakes made serene by autumn.
The clusters of lotuses, having blossomed with their thorny buds revealed and shedding drops of honey like tears of joy, appeared as if their faces were struck with wonder upon the arrival of autumn.
All the lakes, though emaciated by autumn, attained an extreme depth as they were filled by streams of nectar flowing from the blossoming lotuses on every side.

The banks of the noble irrigation channels in the rice fields, covered without interval by heaps of excellent pearls fallen from the mouths of ripe sugarcanes and pomegranates, attained the likeness of the shores of the Tāmraparṇī river.
The forest grounds, interspersed with young sprouts of seeds scattered from pomegranate fruits split open by the ripening of their fruit,
shone as if they were once again covered with emerging cochineal insects.
The *kalamā* rice stalks, bent down by fruits heavy with the ripening of their joy,
appeared as if bowed even more deeply by grief, contemplating the imminent transformation of their own destruction.

With the tips of their horns marked by scattered mud, their hooves like crescent moons wearing away the riverbanks, the bulls, arrogant with rut, repeatedly bellowed as they struck the shores of the streams. (5.55)
In the meantime, the lord of the earth summoned the prince and spoke to him:
"My son, these people desire to witness your practice of the science of weapons."
Having heard that, the ornament of the solar dynasty first replied among the kings:
"Father,
let my training in weapons be observed on the day numbered as the seventh."
Then, when the end of the seventh day had arrived, Prajāpati, together with his kinsmen,
took his seat upon a noble throne in order to observe her training in archery.
With one hand drawing the strung bow and with the other lotus-hand taking up an arrow,
the youth appeared before his preceptor, his body clad in armor.
"Is this the flower-bowed god with his form concealed, or is it the Lord of Spring descended with his bow?"—
such were the conjectures that appeared among the people, whose minds were struck with wonder. (5.60)

That best of heroes, possessing incomparable power, displayed his father’s training in weapons in many varieties— training that was never seen before, surpassing the arts of the world, most wonderful, and marvelous.

Having seen the peerless training in weaponry of the sole kinsman of the world, which had never before existed upon the surface of the earth, the lord of men, whose splendor was equal to that of Indra, held himself in high esteem.
Thus the wise one, the foremost of archers and full of vigor, having displayed his skill in weaponry,
returned to his own home while being loudly praised by the people for his heroic deeds, from the cowherds upwards.
Accompanied by his brides, who were filled with waves of passion and devoted to the great festive celebrations of song and music,
the prince of the king spent several years sporting in pleasure-palaces.
Thus ends the fifth canto in the great poem titled *Padyacūḍāmaṇi*, composed by Buddhaghoṣa.
The Sixth Canto:
A Description of the Spring Season.
The auspicious season of spring appeared, the prelude to the warbling of swarms of bees and cuckoos.
It was a quiver for the arrows of the god whose banner is the makara, and a momentary resting place for the outpourings of the Malaya breeze.
Like the sun, garlanded with fierce rays, terrified as it were by the armor of the fierce-armed Daṇḍadhara, Kāsara, and Saurvabhauma,
he immediately turned his horses from the direction of Yama’s quarter and set out toward the snowy mountain.

By the forest springtime, whose face was radiant with the rising moon and who proclaimed the command of the fish-bannered god (Kāma) through its pure and exceedingly fine garments, the woodland suddenly became possessed of flowers, as if it had been formally wedded.

At that time, the beauty of the fresh and tender sprouts of the flowering trees shone forth as if their tongues had been raised to taste the vital breaths of women who were gripped by an even deeper passion.
Unfastening the bodices of the creepers' ripened foliage, manifesting the horripilation of their clusters of buds,
and tossing about the heavy tresses of their bees, the spring season sported within the garden grounds.

Having mounted his state elephant, which was as gentle as the Malaya breeze, the flower-blossoms became a rain of fresh lotuses for the God of Love who had set forth to conquer the quarters; and the cry of the male cuckoo became the sound of the auspicious conch.
Raising high the pollen from the filaments of flowers by means of the gentle wind blowing through the midst of the forest groves,
it spread through the quarters of the sky like the dust of an army belonging to the God of Love as he prepared for his conquest of the world.

The flock of cuckoos belonging to King Puṣpāyudha roamed through the groves of amorous distraction among the fresh sprouts, as if desiring to gather for himself mango-arrows that were capable of enduring the tumult of battle and were adorned with beautiful feathers.
Having pierced through with his arrows, the hero Māra-subhaṭa bound the branches of great trees within their forked limbs;
there the clusters of blossoms shone like the severed heads of enemies, with swarms of hovering bees appearing like scattered masses of hair.
The clusters of flowers, their faces sealed by bees and their bellies filled with floods of nectar, shone brightly;
they appeared like precious jars brought forth by Time to perform the victory-consecration of the hero, King Māra.
The row of fresh blossoms in the betel-nut grove swayed gently by the sandalwood-scented Malaya breeze,
like a graceful chowrie-staff playfully shaken by the honeyed breath of King Cupid.

Furthermore, in the forest glades where fresh mango buds were blooming, the male cuckoos sang their sweet, clear, radiant, and charming notes in the fifth musical mode, which resembled verses celebrating the heroic exploits of the bodiless Love-god.
The Malaya breeze, a scent-elephant unrestrained by its chains, with rows of bees drawn by the overflowing ichor of honey,
moved slowly as it practiced the sport of breaking down the ramparts upon the mountain peaks of the pride of high-minded women.

The humming of the intoxicated bees swelled forth like the proclamations for the great festival of triumphant love— proclamations made by the gentle breezes acting as royal bards, and by the fragrance of mango blossoms serving as the drums that adorn the elephant of passion.
Spreading out from root to tip on all sides, the mass of young shoots of the forest trees assumed the appearance of a spreading morning glow,
as if to dispel the darkness of pride from the minds of high-minded women.
The forest attained the state of being mothered by rivers through great rivers of honey-nectar essence, flowing from clusters of bees that were incessantly smiling with joy and dripping with nectar.
On the delightful sandy banks of the ocean of nectar, strewn with the pollen of flowers,
the heroic bees, forming circles together with their beloveds, began to drink.
Having placed the female bee, whose song was unceasing, upon a swing made of creepers and fashioned with mechanical ingenuity,
the male bee joyfully rocked her back and forth with breezes arising from the wings of his own body.
Taking up with his mouth the flower-liquor brought by a cluster from an ashoka branch, the bee, like a lover,
made his beloved drink it with flattering words, as their union was interrupted by the crossing of other bees.
Having reached the limbs of the vine-women upon their cluster-breasts, the young bees,
forgetting their restless nature, partook of the drinking of fresh flower-liquor and milk.
Having removed the old string that was worn out by the friction of many battles,
the bees made an unprecedented string for the rod of the bow, which was now a rod of nectar.
Learning from Madhu the song of the peerless one whose origin is unknown,
the young cuckoos slowly warbled melodiously on every branch of the trees.

With their trunk-like arms in the form of branches raised aloft, the mango trees seemed to proclaim to the travelers the command of Śūrpa’s decree through the warbling of cuckoos, which was so pleasing to the ear.

Bending low before him, the buds of full-blown palāśa flowers bore the likeness of golden goads for the god of love, the lord of sea-monsters, who desires to subdue the elephant-king of pride among wanton women.
A row of *palāśa* tree blossoms, variegated by hovering bees,
attained the brilliance of a shimmering mountain ridge that appeared like a mass of smoke.
A cluster of flowers, being pulled away by bees greedy for its fragrance,
appeared like the orb of the full moon being swallowed by the mouth of Rāhu.

Due to its association with serpents that dwell in the embrace of the sandalwood trees on its slopes, the breeze born of the sandalwood mountain repeatedly caused the lover in separation to faint, as if from the company of those very creatures.
In the darkness of a stormy day of honey-droplets,
the intoxicated bee passionately made love with a startle to a female bee who was hastening toward him, incited by the messenger of the forest’s beauty.
The grove of *vakula* trees, having received a sprinkling of honey-like moisture from the mouthfuls of the lips of excellent women,
displayed the beauty of horripilation under the guise of its fresh sprouts.

Like the tinkling of anklets belonging to the Fortune of Spring as she wanders through the mango groves, the sweet warbling of the cuckoos— born from the very essence of melody— provided a feast for the ears of the people.
Having respectfully drunk the wine that filled the lotus-like faces of the women,
the *kesara* tree once again vomited it up under the guise of trickling nectar.
