The gentle breeze from the Malaya mountain performed a long aquatic sport amidst the waves of fragrance from the trees, which filled the interiors of all the directions like rivers.

The god of love, who steals away the intellect of all worldly beings, made the sky resound with the deep twanging of his bowstring as he drew it into a circle; he rained down hundreds of arrows in the form of mango sprouts.
Thus, when the splendor of the spring month had begun, the son of the lord of men, eager to perform a pleasure excursion in the garden,
mounted his chariot and went forth together with the women of the inner apartments.

Then, the deities showed him—whose splendor was like that of Purandara—in succession an old man, a sick man, and one whose life was spent, in order to awaken him with the thought: "This is the time for the Prince's awakening."

Beholding those standing before him in succession, the prince, his mind deeply agitated and his composure disturbed by the thought "What is this?", himself questioned the charioteers who were walking ahead.
Furthermore, presided over by the gods, they explained in detail to the son of the king the causes of dispassion;
they described in succession those transformations of old age and so forth, which were exceedingly difficult to endure.

Having heard their words, the prince, whose disposition was clearly revealed by his profound world-weariness and whose curiosity for strolling in the gardens was restrained, spoke to his charioteer: "Turn back the horses."
Immediately thereafter, before him appeared the Lord of the Gods, a man rich in asceticism whose passions were stilled,
his wide eyes resting upon the very peaks of the waves of the surging ocean of compassion.

His body was as fair as refined gold, his beautiful robes were as crimson as a fragment of coral, the radiance of his face resembled the serene full moon, and his intention was permeated with abundant loving-kindness. // 6.40 //
But beholding him, the foremost of ascetics, the Joy of the Śākyas was filled with wonder;
he asked his charioteers who stood nearby, "Who is this, and what is the excellence of his conduct? (6.41)

"O fortunate one, this is some final [teacher] among the virtuous, pure in mind, of holy conduct, a teacher of the ultimate truth, whose wealth is asceticism, and who has uprooted all defilements along with their latent impressions. (6.42)

The person who has taken refuge in his teaching, having gradually crossed the ocean of birth—fragile as the waves of the transformations of old age and other afflictions—proceeds to the unsurpassed state of nirvāṇa. (6.43)
Thus, by the power of the gods, those heroic ones, for the sake of awakening the son of the protector of the earth,
composed a description of that treasury of asceticism whose deeds transcend the scope of speech and mind.

Having heard these words of the charioteers, the prince— having found the means for his departure from cyclic existence— was inwardly satisfied in mind and desired once more to engage in the pastimes of the garden.
Thus ends the sixth canto in the great poem titled *Padyacūḍāmaṇi*, composed by Buddhaghoṣa.
The Seventh Canto: Siddhārtha’s Entry into the Garden.
Urged on once more by the charioteers with whips in hand, that hero of the world of men [drove] his horse.
He entered a most wonderful grove, delightful to the mind, which brought joy even to the rising Indra.

It was a house of learning for those in their fifth year of study, a quiver of conceptual constructs for the Unborn One, a treasury for the six-footed female bees, and moreover, a pleasure-house for the Fortune of Spring. (7.2)

The trees of the garden, worthy of salutation by all things moving and stationary, bowed down as they approached; with their heads bent low under the influence of the wind, they offered salutations with palms joined like young shoots.
In the midst of the garden, strewn with the sand of falling pollen, sprinkled by the falling nectar of flowers,
and offered oblations by the blossoms that had shed themselves, the Hero wandered about.

Beholding the garden grounds with their graceful movements of the vines, the songs of bees, the sweet warbling of cuckoos, and the sounds of musical instruments, he thought it was like the concert hall of Śambara’s enemy.
Desiring to pluck the flowers of the trees, those lovely women, walking with slow steps,
aroused suspicion in the tree-deities who were present there for the service of the Prince.
Hearing the conversation of those fawn-eyed women dwelling in the pleasure groves,
the voices of spring stood there for a moment in silence, as if feeling ashamed.
"O fair-browed one, do not cause me pain under the pretext of the sound of your anklets," as if pleading thus,
a certain woman gently touched the *aśoka* tree with her foot, tender as a lotus.
The young Ashoka tree, as if unable to endure the touch of the lotus-feet of the young women,
emitted what seemed like the flames of the fire of anger under the guise of its fresh sprouts and blossoms.
A certain woman, through the pleasure of the touch of his lotus-hand— cool as the radiance of nectar-beams—
caused the mango tree to reach the state of having its sprouts and hair stand on end.
Immediately, the mango tree brought forth new sprouts with beautiful leaves tipped by filaments—
causes for pride for that which has no other source, yet thorns to the hearts of the wives of travelers.

A certain woman brought about the state of an *aśoka* tree by means of the juice of aged honey-wine, which was perfumed with *saugandhika* and *indīvara* lotuses, held within her mouth with playful grace, and which she mistook for *kesara*.
With the delightful fragrances of *vakula* trees and heaps of flowers scattered of their own accord,
she fashioned for herself a single, variegated girdle of interlaced creepers, created by her own imagination.
Filling her own mass of hair with clusters of golden flowers brought as offerings and with the noble fragrance of fresh jasmine, she bound it as if it were the quiver of the God of Love.
As she was intent on gathering flowers by force with her sprout-like hand, bending down a branch,
a certain Ashoka tree— as if in anger— obstructed her vision with its pollen.
"How can this harsh thing compete with my delicate hand?"— as if seized by anger at this thought, one woman playfully snapped a tender mango sprout.
One woman, with a particle of *śephālikā* flower pollen that was a brother to the beauty of vermilion,
applied a most lovely *mālatī* leaf-design with grace upon her friend’s forehead.
Gently pulling back the branches of the creepers and plucking a fresh sprout with his hand,
the husband removed the ruby ornament from the neck of another woman and placed it upon her own.
A certain bold woman, while ostensibly placing an ear-ornament into her lover’s ear,
wound her arms around his neck and kissed the radiance of his cheek.
Some lotus-eyed women, enchanting with all their limbs bound with fresh blossoms, bore the likeness of the manifest deities of the five-arrowed god. (7.20)
No one was able to distinguish her friend, who dwelt secretly amidst those creepers radiant with clusters of lovely breasts and possessing shoots as pale-red as lips.
Thus, as the prince sportively frequented the gardens and pleasure groves with his companions,
the thousand-rayed sun ascended to the midst of the sky as if to behold him.
A breeze arrived, heralding midday, skilled at wandering through the mirages that expand upon contact with the fierce heat of the sun, and intensifying the distress of those women.
In the fierce heat of the sun, the shadows of the trees, unable as it were to endure it,
slowly approached the basins at their roots, which had become cool through the repeated sprinkling of water.
Upon the foreheads of the playful women, who were weary from the exertion of their amorous dalliances,
appeared drops of perspiration that were indistinguishable from the sprouts of Pradyumna’s fame.
Showers of drops of water shone upon the cheeks of the broad-hipped women,
appearing like messengers from the lake who had set out in advance to fetch them for their bath.
Having spent his midday heat in the garden grounds, the protector of the central region,
attended by women of excellent complexion, went to a pond for the purpose of sporting in the water.
With its rows of waves stirred by gentle breezes, it had intoxicated royal swans rocking upon them;
with its full-blown white lotuses, it bore bees floating upon a flood of spreading fragrance.
It possessed a sweet current like a stream of honey descending into the hollows of night-lotus buds;
its fish wandered upon a jeweled stage-like expanse formed by a canopy of lofty waves.
In one place, she appeared as if embraced by the Ganges with its full-blown fresh white lotuses;
in another, she shone as if enveloped in crimson by scattered red lotuses.
Beholding the pond, whose quarters were reddened by the pollen of lotuses scattered by the wings of birds and which bore the appearance of a rainy day signaled by its spray, he rejoiced exceedingly.
With his long masses of hair bound fast, and his lotus-like hands radiant with contact with the deer-horns, he,
possessing the power of Varuṇa, descended with his women into the pleasure-park pond.
The pond, having respectfully embraced him who had arrived before it with its hands of waves,
sweetly engaged him in conversation with the delightful cries of its swans.

When it was deeply entered by the beautiful women, the great lake reached its overflowing limit; for how indeed can reservoirs of water, once they have formed an attachment to women, not transgress their bounds? (7.34)
Trembling as if afraid of being struck by the circles of their firm beloveds' breasts,
the rows of waves offered up garlands of pearls under the guise of water droplets.
In the lotus-pool, the prince sported with the women of the inner apartments, whose eyes were like lotuses, as gracefully as Varuṇa does in the ocean with his aquatic nymphs.
With streams of water raised from their beloveds' hands, scattered over the arms of their lovers,
they became for a mere moment the masters of effortless skill in the service of the yak-tail fan.

Some women violently lashed the water with their hands— as if striking a beloved who had committed an offense— its surface bristling with shimmering droplets and its pearl necklaces tossed about by the rhythmic heaving of their jar-like breasts.
While the lotus danced a *tāṇḍava* upon the stage of its waves accompanied by the songs of bees,
other women played the water-drum with their lotus-hands grasping stalks of lotus-fiber.
The lake, crowded with broad-hipped women eager for immersion and emergence,
shone like the ocean interspersed with celestial nymphs appearing here and there.

With his arm, which was encircled by the serpent-king Keyūra and which bore the burden of the earth’s weight, the prince churned the pleasure-pool as the lotus-navelled Lord [Viṣṇu] churned the ocean with Mount Mandara.
Streams of saffron water discharged from machines by the king fell upon the faces of the women,
like the first rays of the sun falling upon groves of lotuses.
The fair-browed women showered him with floods of saffron water sprayed from jeweled syringes;
thus that Tathāgata shone exceedingly, like a *pārijāta* tree in the full splendor of its blossoms.

The stream of water discharged from the machine of the lotus-hand of a certain woman who had revealed her moon-like face fell upon the band of her husband’s jeweled crown, like the Gaṅgā falling upon the mass of matted hair of the Lord Śiva.
Having covered the eyes of one woman with water discharged from a machine operated by his own hand,
the libertine respectfully kissed the bimba-like lower lip of another whose eyes were closed.
Once, a stream of water playfully discharged by her onto the neck of her lover standing nearby shone like a snare set by the God of Love to capture the deer of his heart.

Upon the faces of the fair-browed women there appeared the moonlight of charming smiles; upon their breasts was the loveliness of cascading streams; at their waists was the grace of the celestial river; and from them flowed the torrents of water for bathing.
He washed the face of a certain proud woman with the water from his hands; that very act became the beginning of the ritual libation of water-offerings for the abandonment of her pride.
As they submerged and emerged, the breasts of some women, from which streams of water flowed,
shone like ruddy geese whose lotus stalks have been pulled out by the tips of their beaks.
When her upper garment over her breasts was blown away by the sea breezes, she, feeling ashamed,
concealed the surface of her bosom— marked with the signs of fresh nail-scratches— with a mass of foam.
As she emerged from the water after having submerged herself within it,
her fresh lotus-face shone like the orb of the moon rising from the midst of the ocean.
When their collyrium ornaments were washed away by the waters agitated as they sported in the lake,
the lotus-eyes of the beauties of the inner apartments seemed to sprout anew, as if out of anger.
The breasts of the lotus-eyed women, with the streams of water falling upon them as they sported in the water,
were like the frontal globes of lordly elephants adorned with pearl necklaces, or like mountain peaks with cascading torrents.
Like two great consecration jars for the imperial coronation of the Bodiless One (the God of Love),
the breasts of that lotus-eyed woman drenched [him] with floods of water resting upon their auspicious peaks.
With the ornaments of coral, topaz, lapis lazuli, emerald,
and ruby fallen from the limbs of the lotus-eyed women, even the ocean Kamalākara became a mine of jewels (ratnākara).
Having thus arranged for his residence by the lake, the lotus-eyed prince, together with the women of the harem,
descended from it and entered his dwelling situated on its bank, which was prepared with all the necessary comforts.

There, together with his circle of friends who were devoted to him, the noble one—having fashioned various garments according to his resolve—enjoyed a supreme meal, delightful with its highly flavorful sauces and cooked dishes. (7.57)
The prince sat in the middle of the assembly pavilion, which was provided with variegated silk carpets, strewn with heaps of flowers,
and furnished with an auspicious throne placed within.

There, in the pavilion, the illustrious son of the lord of the earth— the teacher of the three worlds— spent the remainder of the day amidst the incomparable aesthetic delights of the dancing women’s performances, the pleasing sounds of musical instruments, the lute melodies so dear to the ear, and the heart-pleasing tones of the flute. (7.59)
Thus ends the seventh canto in the great poem titled *Padyacuḍāmaṇi*, concerning the life of Buddhaghoṣa.
The Eighth Canto: Description of the Time of Sunset.
In the meantime, the orb of the sun, its crimson glow unabated, fell toward the western quarter.
Like the playful extraction of blue from the expanse of space, as it falls from a jeweled mirror.
The lord of the helmsmen of the western ocean of space, having withdrawn his web of rays,
carried the sun to the shore of the horizon with crystal-like casting-nets.
The orb of the sun, copper-red like a cluster of *aśoka* flowers on the western mountain,
bore the beauty of a coral creeper clinging to the ocean during its churning.

Desiring to undertake his journey to the other world, the radiant sun entered the lotus-pools as if to take leave of his beloved kinsmen, the day-lotuses, by means of hundreds of thousands of reflections.
In due course, the solar orb adorned the middle of the western ocean,
like the jewel named Kaustubha upon the chest of Acyuta, which is dark as an emerald.
The orb of the sun, its disc turned back by the force of the whirlpool from the ocean,
shone as if it had been placed there once more by the Creator to polish away the scratches caused by its circular motion.
"Without me, the ocean shall never overstep its shore, lest it face the onset of universal dissolution"—
as if making this truth manifest with the gestures of his limbs, he took up a mass of glowing, red-hot iron.
At the close of day, the great and precious sun, its light dimmed by the examiner,
was reportedly cast into a mass of coals within the ocean by the submarine fire, as if to rekindle it with its brilliance.

When her husband had set, the twilight— the nurse at the close of day— removed from the vicinity of the lotuses the auspicious thread of the swarms of bees, now that those water-lilies were deprived of their fragrance.
As if from the sorrow of separation from the sun, a swarm of bees emerged from the lotus-faces of the lotus-wives who were shrinking away,
appearing like a column of smoke from the fire of their grief.
Moving nearby in the lotus groves out of greed for fragrance,
the swarm of bees shone like a snare of nooses set by the lotus-wives who were separated from their husbands.
"The sun, my childhood friend, has departed from the impassioned lotus pond and has set"—
as if from such excessive grief, the ruddy goose abandoned his mate and wailed most piteously.
Stretching out between the two directions of day and night,
the twilight shone like a blazing flame, glowing intensely as it was squeezed from both sides by day and night.
Beholding the sun set, the beauty of the sky, as if overwhelmed by excessive grief,
took up the twilight glow as her robe while wearing the stars as a necklace of pearls.
The sprout-like hands of those whose wealth is asceticism, radiant with bracelets of rudrākṣa rosaries,
underwent contraction along with the clusters of lotuses for the sake of the twilight salutation, accompanied by swarms of bees.
The blinding darkness expanded, like the entrance into a subterranean chamber of the earth, while the sky was draped with a blue upper garment of sapphire-like lotuses and bees.
The masses of darkness, like clouds of smoke rising from sun-stones extinguished by moonstones as if they were dripping, filled the sky and the interior of the trees.
The onset of evening, in order to write the excellent descriptions of the moon's stellar qualities,
darkened the slate of the cloudy path with the ink-like varieties of darkness.
Like the mass of light from the throat of Śiva as he performs his twilight *tāṇḍava* dance, the darkness was as if veiling the sky,
like smoke rising from the medicinal plants that were about to blaze forth.
Exceedingly abundant and having dispelled the mass of darkness, they covered the sky,
just as the flood-tides of the Yamunā overwhelm the ocean during the rainy season.
In the houses, streaks of lamplight shone like ear-ornaments of night-blooming campaka flowers;
they appeared as if the splendors of the fleeing sun had been captured as prisoners by the darkness.
Like spies wandering about to investigate the movements of darkness,
groups of jewel-like darknesses shone forth like sparks from the twilight sun.
The sky, jagged with clusters of stars as lovely as hailstones cast down by the showers from clouds of dense nocturnal darkness, possessed the splendor of a forest of night-lotuses.

The path of the stars became strewn with gravel by the clusters of constellations, which possessed a wild splendor like the masses of spray scattered from the trunks of unbridled elephants of darkness.
The sky, variegated by clusters of stars as white as tagara flowers against a background dark as the tamāla tree,
stole the splendor of the ocean after it had been drunk by Agastya and its pearls scattered abroad.
Bearing her son, the moon— who dispels darkness and takes his refuge within the depths of the ocean—
the hundred directions gradually attained a paleness upon their faces.
The garlands of rays rising from the moon hidden within the ocean shone forth,
as if they were streams of water being drunk by the fish through their perforated heads held upward.
The orb of the moon, half-risen, with the beauty of its spot only slightly revealed,
was like a crescent-headed arrow marked with poison, belonging to the source of erotic passion as he sought to conquer the three worlds.
From the whirlpool-like cavity of the navel of Viṣṇu, who is as dark as the tamāla tree and is the ocean of the universe,
there arose the lotus that is the ornament of the circle of the stars, beautiful with bees as its visible markings.
The orb of the moon, rising from the midst of the salt ocean with its surging waves,
bore the likeness of the frontal globes of Airāvata emerging as he was being churned from that very sea.
As the moon, exerting its power, became a discus as red as coral,
it was as if it were filled with jewels drawn from the submarine fire’s crucible by the ocean.
When that lion among kings, having taken his stand with steadfastness upon the slopes, ascends the eastern mountain,
the lords of the earth take refuge in the mountain caves like the elephants of darkness— the spirits of night.
Having had his forefeet struck against the peaks of the eight mountain ranges, the sun fell into the western ocean;
as if terrified by this, the moon, touching the ridges with its rays, ascended the first mountain.
The full-moon disc, crimson with its new rising,
shone at the edge of the sky like a single mark applied by the liquid mineral pigment presiding over the seal of evening.

The Lord of the Night, with his sprout-like rays, fastened upon the lotus-stalks at the edge of the lily-pool a garland of auspicious threads consisting of rows of bees, as if for those lotuses who were filled with curiosity.
Having heard the song of the female bees— which was like nectar to the ears— the moon, as if having drunk that nectar,
bestowed upon them a multitude of sealed night-lily buds filled with honey.
The splendor of the sky shone with clusters of stars scattered like fresh blossoms from the Night-Maiden, whose tresses of darkness had become loosened by the touch of her husband’s hand.
Studded with pearls released from conch shells resembling the moon’s orb in its full maturity,
and shimmering like the spray of the celestial river, the splendor of the sky gleamed as if filled with stars.
While her husband, the moon, who is full of affection, occupied the surface of his bed in the sky,
the dark garment of darkness was cast away from the midst of the heavens by the fair-limbed lady of the night.
Just as the lord of beasts consumes the *kālakūṭa* poison, or as the jar-born Agastya drinks up the lord of rivers,
the moon, seizing the deep darkness with its sprout-like rays, swallowed it whole.
As if out of sorrow at their separation, the moon comforted with his hand the night-lily— pale-bodied, with bees for its hanging tresses, and smeared with the pollen of its nectar-scented flowers.
In the waters of the evening tide, which shimmered like jeweled mirrors, the moon’s orb appeared as a reflection;
Varuṇa, the lord of the waters, suspected that the ocean—the sole mine of jewels—had been marked with a seal by him.

The beauty of the lunar orb was perceived within, possessing the luster of a young *tāla* tree shimmering inside; it appeared as if sealed by the liquid venom from the fangs of Rāhu, whose mouth was wide open down to the corners of his lips.
The reflection of the moon, the tutelary deity of the night-lotus family, appeared clearly, its deer-mark visible;
it shone like a circle of whirlpools produced by the union of the daughter of the mountain-king with the Yamunā.
The orb of the moon shone exceedingly, its light unbroken though the deer-mark quivered within;
it was like a pair of ivory earrings with an emerald set in their centers, belonging to the night, that woman with the beautiful eyebrows.
The orb of the nectar-rayed moon, soiled within and appearing like a mirror whose surface is tarnished by clouds and wind;
its interior mottled by the spreading radiance from his neck—how it resembles the alms-bowl of the skull-handed Lord Śiva!
When the evening had become clear, the son of the protector of men, his splendor of auspicious ornaments fashioned by Tvaṣṭṛ,
returned once more to his own palace, attended on all sides by courtesans with jeweled lamps.
Thus ends the eighth canto in the great poem titled *Padyacūḍāmaṇi*, composed by Buddhaghoṣa.
The Ninth Canto: The Lustration of the Prince.
Having arrived and taken his seat upon an auspicious throne in the midst of the palace, the prince—
Assisted by his mother and nurses, he undertook the waving of the ritual lamp.
Then the son of the great king of kings, possessing the powerful build of a lion, stood upon the pavilion in order to ascend the throne.
Before him, the beautiful women of Vāravaṇā, with their sweet forms, began to display a wondrous display of dance.
Though their performance was captivating with its graceful gestures and their new songs were fresh, his heart remained unattached, and he gave himself over to internal reflection.
Then that prince shone with yak-tail fans raised by the immortals,
like the ocean with its waves tossed up by the wind.
The circle of the earth shone with banners and jeweled flags,
like the sky enveloped by many streaks of lightning.
The sky, enveloped by the great coils of smoke from black aloe-wood incense,
shone like the netherworld (rasātala) teeming with hundreds of black serpents.
The sky became filled with the sounds of many drums, which, filling the belly of the universe, deafened the quarters of the horizon.
Like the celestial nymphs of Airāvata upon the stage of the sky,
the sounds of the clouds' instruments performed an uninterrupted sequence of *tāṇḍava* dances.
By means of their faces with their darting, moving glances,
the surface of the sky became as if it possessed a thousand moons.
And the Vidyādharas and Gandharvas, with lutes held in their hands and their mouths eloquent with ancient legends, set out before him.
The masses of mandāra flowers scattered by the hand of Mahendra fell like stars, displaced by the upheaval of the world.
Thus propitiated by the gods, he traversed a path of thirty yojanas and reached the ninth river.
Thick with lotus stalks licked by female swans, its quarters made resonant by the deep roar of crocodiles. (9.14)
The sky was speckled with stars that resembled the spray from the waves,
and the breeze was made fragrant by the scent of lotuses.
The circle of waves reached up to their necks, shimmering with the essence of the swaying circles of ripples. 9.16.
It was colored by the filaments of clusters of white lotuses scattered about by fish,
and rippled with the flowing honey-juice exuding from blossoming lotuses.
As if spreading out a bridge of virtues to cross the great ocean,
he crossed that river by means of a vehicle joined with reflection.
Having crossed it, he dismounted from his horse on its bank and,
having given the ornaments and the mount, he sent them back in concealment.
The foremost among men received that refinement of ascetic wealth which had arisen at the beginning of the eon and was gathered by the primordial Brahmā.
Having taken up the ascetic’s attire, which was woven from many virtues,
and having clothed himself in it, he established his steadfastness in austerity.
Then, having beheld Lokeśa initiated toward the direction of Indra,
he attained a whiteness as if through joyful, gentle smiles.
By the command of that Teacher, the Lord of all the worlds, as it were,
the sky assumed a twilight-pink hue at the direction of Indra.
To behold that crest-jewel of the Śākya lineage, the sun,
stationed upon the peak of the shore, ascended the eastern mountain.
As if commanding him, "In this way, you must dispel the ignorance of the worlds," the sun drove away the darkness.
And by saying, "In this very way, let there be the light of knowledge for the three worlds," the Maker of Light (the Sun) seemed to manifest his radiance as if giving this command.
When the lord of mountains had been initiated, the other mountains, as if filled with despondency,
donned bark garments under the pretext of the morning sunlight.
As if from the very rising of the kinsman of the sun, that unique ocean of awakening,
all the beds of lotuses assumed the seal of blossoming.
With their lotuses closed like hands joined in reverence, all the beds of night-lotuses stood as if with palms pressed together in salutation toward him who had accomplished his purpose.
Like stars eclipsed by the brilliance of the sun, those heretics were overwhelmed by the splendor of this teacher of the true path and became lusterless.
As if to provide space for that mass of his fame,
every gap in the quarters of the sky attained extreme vastness.
Having seen Siddhārtha’s face, which was like a cool-rayed moon shining even by day,
the moon itself became lusterless, as if overcome by shame.
As if by the mere sight of that sole teacher of the world, the radiant sun,
its splendor of rising glow departed, entered the hermitage through the sky.
Satisfied by the flavor of the renunciation he had attained after hundreds of longed-for desires,
the teacher spent several days on its bank.
Then one day, the Primal Mendicant, hungry and seeking alms,
traveled a long distance and arrived at the city of Bimbasāra.
[He saw] mountains whose boundaries were surpassed by massive stone palaces,
and oceans that had been turned into mere ponds by the moats of Pātāla’s unfathomable depth.
The surface of the earth was embraced by the tips of the hooves of mares,
while the streets were made muddy by the rut of the intoxicated lords of rutting elephants.
[She saw the city] where female swans alighted upon the balconies of the ruby palaces,
and which was resplendent with streaks of smoke billowing from the mouths of its windows.
Its green borders were made resonant by the jingling of the tips of the golden bells on the young trees,
and its mansions were adorned with the crests of banners fluttered by the gentle breeze.
It was rich with the jeweled archways of the smiling bows of Valāri,
and it featured garlands of salutation formed by the sprouts of creeping vines along its streets.
It had a middle girdled by the expanse of broad streets, shining with its center,
and possessed well-proportioned side-branches in the form of pleasure-pools and ripples.
There, the crest-jewel of those whose wealth is asceticism, the Leader, wandered slowly from street to street to collect alms. (9.42)
Upon beholding this Lord of Sages, who dispels all delusion,
everyone— both the ignorant and the wise— fell into the sleep of infatuation.
Even the enemy of Manobhava (Śiva) produced *manobhava* (passionate desire) in them, whose eyes were made to expand wide, free from the blinking and closing of their lids.
There, having taken up alms, he who was well-versed in the steps of training quickly took refuge in a mountain peak situated nearby. (9.45)
It was enchanting with black-necked cuckoos warbling in the vicinity,
and it had the herds of elephants pulverized by the blows of lions' claws.
Adorned by the lord of serpents, whose coiled body resembles the trunk of an elephant, where flocks of peacocks have commenced their frantic dance, and which is named Pāṇḍara; (9.47)
It was a place where clouds resting upon the expanse of its vast peaks served as travelers, and where the great boulders were like duplicates of the roaming, intoxicated elephants.
The hollows of the sky were split apart by the tips of massive boulders,
and it was strewn with pearls from the tusks of elephants seized by the hands of five-faced lions.
Its rocky surfaces were washed by the torrents of mountain streams,
and at the edge of its slopes sported the commanders of the Pulinda hosts.
Having bathed in a nearby pond, Siddhārtha stood upon a stone slab on its bank and partook of the essence of the alms-food.
On the following day, having gone out from that city and performed the rite of collecting alms-food within the town, he reached a nearby forest.
Dwelling near a pond, on the bank of a river, on a mountain, and in a forest, this venerable one passed many days. (9.53)
In auspicious groves of asceticism, he of steadfast heart practiced even those austerities that are difficult to accomplish, for the sake of pacifying the sufferings of cyclic existence.
"Without having attained the state of nirvāṇa, even through difficult practices, what means could there be for its sake?"—thus he became distressed. (9.55)
Once, at dawn, the treasury of virtuous conduct beheld five dreams that revealed the ripening of his fortune for the perfections (pāramitās).
Having seen, understood, and reflected upon the meaning of the dream, the wise one resolved:
"This very day I shall attain final liberation. (9.57)
Having performed his morning rites and awaited the time for alms,
he sat beneath a banyan tree where he had prepared an offering of honor.
Then a certain large-eyed woman, being devoted to prayer, was constantly intent upon offering milk-rice to a deity residing there. (9.59)
Out of that very suspicion, she gave him the milk-rice in a bowl;
taking it, the Great Being went to the bank of the Nairañjanā.
Having bathed in her waters, which were as pure as the autumnal night sky, the wise sage ate the milk-rice served in a golden vessel.
Then, [he entered] that place which shone with the playful morning sunlight upon the young sprouts,
and whose green borders were made resonant by the charming warbling of cuckoos.
Where bees were rendered restless by the swaying of creepers shaken by a gentle breeze,
and where the cuckoos rejoiced in tasting the sprouts of young mango trees.
In that place fragrant with the nectar dripping from the buds of the *mandāraka* tree,
where the breeze carrying the scent of rut stirred up a thrill like a budding plantain tree.
On the excellent path made tawny by clusters of full-blown blossoms,
travelers were startled by the "hum" of wandering bees that sounded like the roar of a thunderbolt.
In that place, the ground was dusty with the mass of pollen scattered by the wings of birds,
and its surface was mired in the thick honey-nectar of mango blossoms.
In the jeweled pavilion of the sovereign empire of the spring season, where the wind was filled with the most excellent blossoming jasmine creepers; (9.67)
Having stayed in a grove of *sāla* trees abounding in *tāla*, *tamāla*, and *hintāla* trees,
the leader of men passed the midday heat.
When the end of the day had arrived and only one watch remained,
the Blessed One, of vast prowess, rose up and attained enlightenment.
Taking the darbha grass offered by Brahmā with his own hands,
the best of teachers scattered it upon the ground of the Bodhi tree toward the east.
There, a great throne appeared— the invincible couch— which was exceedingly delicate yet impenetrable to the pride of Kandarpa.
He ascended his lofty throne, marvelous like the enemy of Ananga (Śiva), just as the sun ascends the eastern mountain, awakening all people.
The gods began to praise him, who had ascended the seat of enlightenment and possessed unswerving virtues, yet who remained beyond the reach of speech and mind.
Homage to the ocean of excellent qualities, the kinsman of the sun;
homage to the bridge across the ocean of saṃsāra, the banner of the sages.
Homage to the one who removes all afflictions and possesses all virtues;
homage to the knower of the meaning of all principles, the proponent of non-duality. // 9.75 //
Homage to you, O Blessed One, whose eyes are overflowing with waves of the flood of compassion, and who are the treasury of good fortune. 9.76
You alone are capable of shattering the pride of Kandarpa, and no one else;
for who indeed, other than the five-faced one, is able to subdue an elephant? (9.77)
You alone are the hero in crushing the haughty heretics who are difficult to restrain; by whom else could the ocean be churned without Mount Mandara? // 9.78 //
You alone are the hero in swallowing the ocean of existence;
for who else, indeed, is a wise man in sucking up the sea except for the pot-born Agastya?
In this matter of awakening the girdle of Śroṇī, you alone are skilled;
for who else but the moon can cause the laughter of the lily pond? // 9.80 //
O Lord, you alone are capable of completely exhausting the afflictions of existence;
what other than the sun could possibly have the power to remove darkness? (9.81)
Through these hymns of praise, which caused the emergence of his increasing virtues,
Manmatha heard that the Buddha had ascended to the foot of the tree of enlightenment.
Having heard this, the Mind-born One, his inner soul agitated, resolved to conquer that lowest of men who was detached from worldly desires.
"What means might I have in this world?"—thus he was quickly consumed by the fever of anxiety. // 9.83 //
Thus ends the ninth canto in the great poem titled *Padyacūḍāmaṇi*, composed by the venerable Buddhaghoṣa.
The Tenth Canto: A Description of Māra’s Mobilization.
In the meantime, having stationed himself densely at the foot of the Bodhi tree, Māra, filled with agitation and desiring to lead an army against the Lord of Sages, [prepared himself].
Having mounted his rutting elephant named Girimekhala, Ananga set forth with a multitude of summoned troops.
Having emerged, with his great army— which filled the hollows of the distant quarters with its roar, which was as terrifying as a thunderclap,
and which struck fear into all people— the bodiless god (Ananga) slowly descended to the earth.
The sound of Māra’s excellent war-conch, filling the mouths of hundreds of agitated conch-blowers,
did not cause distress to the Ocean-dweller, whose own Pāñcajanya had been constantly cherished in the midst of battle.

The spreading, terrible roar of the thunderbolt, which filled the entire belly of the atmosphere, produced only joy for the god whose ears were treated to a festival by that sound; it was like the roar of the trident-bearer’s own formidable shout.
The force of the fierce winds, mocking the circles of Vaitaṇḍa elephants, shattered the massive boulders of the principal mountain ranges;
the entire horizon was made to surge by the waves of horses leaping with high, tossing leaps, as if risen from the ocean at the time of universal dissolution.
The surface of the earth was rent asunder by the streams from the rims of the wheels of the circles of rushing chariots;
and the dense darkness of dust, thick enough to shroud the underworld, was shattered by the thunderbolt-like falling of the infantry’s feet.
The sky was turned green by the rising shadows of the terrifying black swords brandished in their hands,
while the entire world was deafened by the forceful twanging of the bowstrings from the forest of bows drawn with effortless ease.
The sky bore its name in truth through the sound of a terrible clamor from the beating of incomparable, fearsome drums;
meanwhile, the path of the clouds was made formidable by the spray of hissing breath emitted from the openings of his trunk-like baskets.
The flood of the Sindhu river was turned into a mere mouthful by the mass of dust incessantly swelling from the surface of the earth;
the interior of every cave was filled with the lion-roars of the vanguard heroes and the thundering of their battle-cries.

With its fourfold army moving in succession— the wheels of which were urged on by the command of the enraged Flower-Arrowed One (Kāma), and which brought about the wondrous arrival of the autumn season through the swarms of white chowries being vigorously waved— it set forth.

The interior of the pavilion was filled with the resounding blasts of kettledrums, which were indistinguishable from the deep and terrible thundering of masses of clouds gathering at the end of an eon, and which served as musical instruments for the god of love.

In the worlds, the tumultuous sound of the kettledrums arising from Madana’s expedition caused supreme distress to the preeminent serpents, whose agitated vision was blinded by the rising masses of dust from the delighted armies.
When the mass of dust from the armies completely blinded the quarters of the sky, even as the light of the multitude of clouds [was obscured],
the celestial chariots of the gods, having lost their way like boats upon a surging river, wandered aimlessly through the path of the deities.

Amidst the great cloud of dust raised by the soldiers, the moving celestial chariots of the gods shone like fragments of the cosmic egg tossing repeatedly upon the floodwaters of the ocean during its cataclysmic dance of destruction.
Terrified by the force of the winds agitated at the end of an aeon, and overwhelmed by the army of Kandarpa, which was as formidable as those winds,
the oceans— under the guise of the mass of thick, rising dust— seemed as if they had leapt up into the sky.
Like darknesses that had entered the caves of mountains split by the tusks of the enemy’s victorious elephants,
masses of dust from the army— delightful as bees and expanding with unceasing force— enveloped the sky.
The cavern of the sky was filled and shone with the exceedingly vast floods of dust from the immeasurable armies;
it appeared as if it were embracing the middle of the salt ocean, whose entire expanse had been inundated by the currents of the Yamunā.
With their towering masses of thick dust covering the earth and overspreading the exceedingly brilliant circle of the sky,
they were like the women of the quarters who, out of fear of the falling arrows of Love, had donned dark blue cloud-mantles.
When the floodwaters of the oceans were swallowed up by the mass of dust and he was able to move about freely everywhere,
the Slayer of Kaiṭabha, mistaking it for the end of the eon, desired once again to withdraw the entire universe into his belly.
The oceans, already swallowed by the harsh dust raised from the earth trampled by the charging horses,
became even more redundant in their waters through the floods of rut-fluid trickling from the temples of the intoxicated elephants.
The moon, the son of the ocean who plundered the ocean’s wealth and who arose as the dust in the army of the god of love,
was cast aside by the lotus-leaf as if out of anger harbored within, thinking, "This is my enemy's kinsman."
As if unable to endure the exceedingly fierce insult directed at the banner of his own lineage,
he vanished amidst the dense columns of dust from Kāma’s army, which had rendered all directions shrouded in deep darkness.
With the thick darkness of the dust-clouds raised by the advancing army, with the lightning-flashes of hundreds of trembling elephant-standards,
and with the hailstones of foam-droplets from the cavalry, it became like the onset of the rainy season, bringing joy to all.
As the unbridled dust spread through the circle of the quarters, thickening the gloom and obstructing the space of the sky,
the surface of the earth became like the netherworld, while the abode of the virtuous became like the realm of the earth itself.
When the entire mass of pollen rose high from the surface of the earth, which was trampled by the hooves of the cavalry,
the mountains became truly "earth-bearers" (mountains), while even Śeṣa became merely a bearer of the weight of a garland of hoods.

When the mass of dust raised by the army, resembling the exposed face-cloths of the elephants of the quarters, began to expand, the oceans instantly became filled with mud; likewise, the clouds in the sky became bearers of mire.

The elephants of the quarters, having breached their ramparts, made a gap for the dust to spread beyond the Cakravāḍa mountain— that immeasurable dust which had drunk up the waters of all the oceans of the Makara-source and filled the skies throughout the reaches of space— just as if they were clearing a path outside the world-encircling range.
In that ocean of an army, with its great current of victorious infantry, the lordly elephants appeared like submerged mountain ranges;
the lofty horses shone intensely like surging masses of waves, and the chariots were like circles of ships. 10.28.
In the center, the stainless banners of Māra’s victory, adorned with the sight of a leaping makara emblem, shone brilliantly;
they appeared like the wives of his city-dwellers captured as prisoners after he had conquered the ocean with his own sea of forces.
With his body enveloped in a soiled cloak of smoke arising from the great fire of indignation blazing within him,
he made himself exceedingly terrifying, possessing many thousands of arms and grasping various weapons.

The god of love, whose limits are unseen, ordered his own army to be marshaled— an army terrifying in appearance, which filled the hollows of the mountains and the reaches of all directions, and resembled the ocean agitated at the end of an eon as it was being drawn back.
Surrounded by his retinues of immeasurable power who covered the entire surface of the earth to its very limits,
the Self-Born approached the bull among sages, whose fortitude was unshakable as he sat upon the sacrificial altar-platform of his seat of enlightenment.
Having donned his most beautiful robes as armor and mounted the neck of his noble elephant of yoga,
the Flower-Armed One (Kāmadeva), his eyes reddened by flashing indignation, began to fight that heap of unshakable heroism.
In his presence—that ocean of the nectar of tranquility and self-restraint—the pure arrows of Smara were rendered powerless.
What indeed cannot be accomplished by those of pure soul who have not sought the elevation of the fruits of their giving, and who have established the side of imperishability? (10.34)
While he, an ocean of fortitude, was assuming a body composed of patience and possessed a power as fierce as the heat of the sun,
the arrows of the Flower-Armed God, their own progress blunted, turned back like malevolent spells (*kṛtyā*) and struck him instead.
The hosts of Māra’s searchers, becoming well-disposed and gathering together with their noble wings spread, approached that man of great bounty;
yet, who would grant a gift to one whose actions are devoid of virtue? (10.36)

The sharp arrows dispatched by the Fish-bannered One, who stood with his long bow drawn into a circle, reached the Buddha and were transformed into flowers; for what can the company of the virtuous not accomplish, like a celestial creeper? (10.37)

Having approached the sovereign of sages, whose heart was tranquil, even though his arrows were devoid of any special power of consciousness, they immediately became blunt; yet that enemy of Śambara, his heart consumed by fury, did not become softened.
Those arrows, though successful against the mind-born god of love, became fruitless upon reaching him whose heart was at peace;
for when fate turns its face away, alas, everything goes to ruin, even if it has already come into one's hand. 10.39.
Thus, when all his arrows— capable of overwhelming the three worlds— had become useless, alas! Māra, his heart blinded by the grip of enmity, commanded the wind of the great dissolution to crush him.

A great wind, having received its bath from the abundance of water rising from the divine river that flows down from the very roots [of the trees], and possessing the pollen of flowers gathered as if for the purpose of worship, approached the unshaken Sage.
Faced with that Lord of Sages, who was heavy with the burden of all virtues, even he of great speed was unable to shake him;
this is not surprising, for the power of a forest fire, which devours every kind of wood, does not fail even in the face of water.
Thus, when even those vast weapons such as great winds and clouds proved futile,
the Flower-Armed One (Kāma) further desired to conquer that primal man with the arrows of his words, which pierce the vital points of the heart.
"This seat is not yours; it is mine. Arise and depart quickly from here at once!
For I alone have fulfilled the supreme perfections, and my great army is the witness to that," she said.
Stretching out his sprout-like hand from his lap, the foremost mendicant, whose power was born of intense austerity, spoke these words:
"Māra fled from there with a great force, terrified, his parasols, chariots, banners, and blankets all fallen away."
Thereafter, the women of Māra, casting languid glances and adorned with tinkling jeweled anklets and bracelets upon their feet,
suddenly gathered and performed an exceedingly grand *tāṇḍava* dance upon the spacious, square central area of that ground.

Beholding the joy of the Śākya clan, who was unshakable and whose taste for internal meditative concentration was undisturbed, the women of desire with timid eyes uttered words that were nectar to the ears and composed of piteous syllables. (10.47)

How can the ancient chronicles say that you plucked out your pair of eyes and gave them to the best of the twice-born, when you were unable even to grant her a glance—she who was overwhelmed by the falling arrows of Love? (10.48)

How will you rescue the entire world from the ocean of existence, when you yourself are so unskilled at rescuing even me—who am great, who am thus distressed by mental anguish in the sea of the god whose banner is the great makara, and who am destitute of support? (10.49)

"Having seen our most faultless grace, which even causes the shaking of the head in praise to recede far away, how can the lords of poets say that he cut off your head—thereby uprooting the power of his enemies—and gave it to you? (10.50)

"O Lord of the meritorious! If you desire to attain the state of Supreme Manhood, what need have you for ascetic penances? Place one of our daughters upon your broad chest, which is as vast as a slab of Mount Meru. (10.51)
If you desire a noble lineage or wish to attain the state of a supreme lord, you are capable of achieving it through austerities;
yet, mount some lovely woman with beautiful curls upon your left side—she whose glances are as broad as lotus petals.

Truly, only the fortunate become the recipients of the glances of those fair-eyed women—glances whose playful movements cause the eyes to blossom with joy, which seize the pride of clusters of lotuses, and whose radiance is revealed by manifest smiles. 10.53.

What else could the speech of deer-eyed women be but nectar—speech that possesses the playful charm of a cuckoo’s call drawn forth, that is drunk by ears opened wide to its very corners of vision, and that is beautiful with wondrous turns of expression, providing immediate bliss? (10.54)

For indeed, the nectar of the lips of women— which is an elixir capable of sustaining one through endless drinking, which is delightful to the mind as a constant accompaniment to the arising of the heat of passion, and which is never exhausted— brings about a state of being tasted only for those men who possess merit.

Having beheld the Buddha, whose mental state was unshakable, with such incomparable sequences of dance infused with the flavors of graceful emotions and the playful charms of speech, the young women turned back in shame and departed.

Thus, at the foot of the auspicious Bodhi tree, the noble Siddhārtha— having established the beautiful-eyed Sambodhiprasādā in a state parched by the victorious activity of the flower-bowed god of love,
and having utterly eradicated the enemies that are the mental afflictions which had long resided within him— attained his goal.
He was foolishly consecrated to the task of protecting the family estate of Muktikṣetra. // 10.58 //
Thus ends the tenth canto in the *Siddhārthacarita*, a great poem titled *Padyacūḍāmaṇi*, composed by Buddhaghoṣa.
